title: Waking seeds: why seeds from one packet do not wake together
playtest: Read step by step as a parent and child in a city flat would use it. The depth test, the waking curve, the pale search and the Dry Vault use tumblers, plates and kitchen things only. Not yet run at home: please check these. First, the exact hours at which moong roots show depend on the room, so in a cool room add counts at 60 and 72 hours. Second, in the depth test the deep mustard cup usually shows no shoots, and the dug-up seeds usually show thin pale shoots, but the numbers vary with the soil. Third, rubbed tamarind seeds should swell and gain weight in a day or two while untouched ones stay hard, but some untouched seeds may swell slowly. Fourth, the iodine test on a six-day sprout may show only a small difference from the soaked chana, because a seedling empties the store slowly, and the activity says so. Fifth, the jackfruit activity only works in season and takes three weeks, and the result can vary. Sixth, the Rain Door amounts of water may need adjusting for your cup and sand. Seventh, the tamarind activity can use a press score if you have no gram scale. The two games have their rules and cards written out in full, and Wake or Wait can be played alone against the deck.

summary.text: Thirty moong seeds from one packet lie on the same wet cloth, in the same warm room. Some have a white root by the next morning. Some wake a day later, and a few wait for days. Your child counts the wake-ups every few hours and draws the waking curve. Then your child tests how deep a tiny seed and a big seed can be sown, what happens to a shoot that never finds light, and why a hard seed coat is like a locked door.
summary.art: Thirty moong seeds in three rows on a damp cloth on a steel plate, some with white roots, some swollen, some still green and wrinkled.

intro.hook: Put 30 moong seeds from one packet on a wet cloth. Leave them in a warm room. Look again after 12 hours. Some seeds already have a white root. Others have not moved at all. They had the same water, the same warmth and the same air. Why did they not wake together?
intro.text: A packet of seeds looks like a crowd of identical things. But no two seeds are exactly alike, and every seed has their own way of waking. In this unit you count the wake-ups hour by hour. You also find out how deep a seed can be buried, why a seedling in the dark grows long and pale, and what a tamarind seed needs before water can get in. In the end you will see why a packet that wakes all at once might be a bad thing for the seeds.
intro.art: A steel plate with a damp cloth and thirty moong seeds, with a clock beside it showing 12 hours later and a few white roots poking out.

outcomes: I can count how many seeds in a test sprouted, turn the count into a percentage, and say why a test uses many seeds.
I can explain that seeds from one packet wake at different times, and why that spread of wake-up times helps the seeds as a group.
I can explain dormancy, and name at least three different things that wake a dormant seed.
I can explain why a seed with a bigger food store can be sown deeper than a tiny seed.
I can describe two ways a seedling comes up, with the seed leaves lifted into the air or left under the soil.
I can explain what happens to a seedling that grows without light, and what light changes.
I can explain how dry and cold slow a seed's ageing, and why some seeds, such as mango and jackfruit, cannot be stored dry.

terms.meaning: A seed is viable if the baby plant inside is alive. A viable seed can sprout when they get what they need.
terms.example: Fresh moong is viable. Boiled moong is not.
terms.art: A split moong seed with a tiny living baby plant marked, next to a boiled one with a grey cross.

terms.meaning: Out of every 100 seeds you test, the number that sprout. A packet that says 80 percent means that 80 of every 100 seeds sprouted in the seller's test.
terms.example: If 24 of 30 moong seeds sprout, that is 80 of every 100, or 80 percent.
terms.art: A grid of 100 small circles with 80 of them coloured green and 20 left empty.

terms.meaning: How fast seeds sprout. Seeds with a fast rate show roots early. Seeds with a slow rate take many days.
terms.example: Moong in a warm kitchen has a fast rate. Tamarind has a slow rate.
terms.art: Two clocks, one showing moong sprouting after one day and one showing tamarind sprouting after many days.

terms.meaning: When a seed is alive and has water, warmth and air, but still does not sprout. The seed is holding back until the right sign comes.
terms.example: Apple seeds are dormant until they have been through weeks of cold.
terms.art: A seed lying in damp soil, with a closed padlock drawn on the seed coat.

terms.meaning: Rubbing, scratching or thinning a hard seed coat so that water can get in. The word comes from scar.
terms.example: Rubbing a tamarind seed on rough sandpaper lets water in.
terms.art: A tamarind seed being rubbed on a nail file, with a dull patch on its shiny coat.

terms.meaning: A spell of cold that some seeds need before they will wake. Scientists call it stratification.
terms.example: Apple seeds wake much better after weeks in a cold place such as a fridge.
terms.art: Apple seeds in a damp tissue inside a bag on a fridge shelf.

terms.meaning: A chemical messenger made by a living body. It travels from one part to another and tells cells what to do. Plants have hormones too.
terms.example: A hormone called gibberellin tells the food store of a seed to start working.
terms.art: A tiny baby plant sending dotted arrows to the big food-store halves of a bean.

terms.meaning: The first root of a baby plant, the part that comes out of the seed first.
terms.example: The white tail on a sprouted moong seed is a radicle.
terms.art: A sprouted moong seed with the radicle marked as a short white tail.

terms.meaning: When the fat seed leaves are lifted into the air and turn green. Scientists call this epigeal germination.
terms.example: Moong and rajma lift their seed leaves above the soil.
terms.art: A moong seedling with two fat seed leaves held up above the soil line.

terms.meaning: When the seed leaves stay under the soil and only the shoot comes up. Scientists call this hypogeal germination.
terms.example: Chana and peas leave their seed leaves under the soil.
terms.art: A chana seedling with only a green shoot above the soil and the seed halves visible below.

terms.meaning: The green substance in leaves that catches sunlight so the plant can make food.
terms.example: A seedling grown in the dark has almost no chlorophyll, so they are pale.
terms.art: A magnified green leaf cell with many small green discs inside.

terms.meaning: A seedling that grew in the dark. The seedling is long, thin, pale and floppy, because they spent their food stretching to find light. Scientists call this an etiolated seedling.
terms.example: The long white shoots of bean sprouts sold in markets are grown in the dark.
terms.art: Two seedlings side by side, a tall thin pale one and a short sturdy green one.

terms.meaning: A small part that stands for a bigger whole. A bigger sample gives a steadier answer.
terms.example: A seed lab tests 400 seeds to say how well a whole sack will sprout.
terms.art: A handful of seeds taken out of a big sack and set on a tray.

terms.meaning: How much of a seed's weight is water. A dry seed in a jar might be about one-tenth water.
terms.example: Chana kept in a damp monsoon kitchen slowly takes in water, and the moisture content of the chana rises.
terms.art: A seed with a small water drop drawn inside the seed, and a scale beside the seed showing a percentage.

terms.meaning: A safe store of many kinds of seeds, kept dry and cold so that they stay alive for many years.
terms.example: India has a national seed bank in New Delhi. Farmers like Rahibai Popere keep village seed banks of old local crops.
terms.art: A cold room with rows of labelled jars and packets on steel shelves.

terms.meaning: A seed that stays alive when dried and kept cold. Scientists call this an orthodox seed.
terms.example: Moong, chana, wheat and rice can be dried and stored for years.
terms.art: A jar of dry chana on a shelf, with a calendar showing many years.

terms.meaning: A kind of seed that dies on drying out, so these seeds must be sown fresh. Scientists call this a recalcitrant seed.
terms.example: Jackfruit and cocoa seeds are wet-keeping seeds.
terms.art: A jackfruit seed in damp soil, and a shrivelled dried one beside the first with a cross.

explanations.concept: A germination test: counting how many seeds wake
explanations.definition: A germination test counts how many seeds in a sample sprout. The count is turned into a germination percentage, which is how many seeds out of every 100 would sprout.
explanations.description: Seed sellers and seed labs test their seeds before they sell them. They put seeds on damp paper in warm conditions and count the ones with a root. Suppose 24 of 30 seeds sprout. 30 seeds make three lots of 10, and 24 makes three lots of 8, so 8 out of every 10 seeds sprouted. That is 80 out of every 100, or 80 percent. A seed packet in India usually carries this number, so a farmer knows how many seeds to sow. If the packet says 80 percent and you want 40 plants, you sow 50 seeds. A real seed lab does not test just a few seeds. Many labs test four lots of 100 seeds, and compare the lots. A small test can mislead, because one or two odd seeds change a small count a lot.
examples: If 9 of 10 seeds sprout, that is 90 percent. If 18 of 20 sprout, that is also 90 percent.
A packet says 80 percent. To get 40 plants you sow 50 seeds, because 8 out of every 10 sprout.
A seed lab tests 400 seeds, in four lots of 100, so that one odd lot does not fool them.
explanations.art: A seed test tray with four lots of 100 seeds, a count written under each lot, and a percentage on a label.

explanations.concept: Seeds in one packet do not wake together
explanations.definition: Seeds from the same plant, in the same packet, wake at different times. A few sprout early, most sprout in the middle and a few sprout late. The running total is the number of seeds that have sprouted so far. If you plot the running total against time, the line looks like a letter S stretched out sideways, which people call a lazy S.
explanations.description: Every seed is a little different from every other seed. One was a bit bigger, one sat nearer the middle of the pod, one has a coat that is a little thicker. So water reaches the baby plant at different speeds, and the baby plants are ready at different speeds. You see this when you count a plate of moong every few hours. The running total starts slowly, speeds up in the middle and slows down at the end. Scientists call this a germination curve. The time when half the seeds have sprouted is a handy number. It tells you how fast the batch is. The gap between the first and last seed tells you how spread out the batch is. Old seeds are usually slower and more spread out than fresh seeds.
examples: On a plate of 30 moong, 4 might have roots at 12 hours, 15 at 24 hours, 24 at 36 hours and 28 at 48 hours.
A packet that is two years old often starts later, finishes with fewer seeds, and has a longer gap between the first and last seed.
Two plates of seeds from the same packet give similar curves, but never exactly the same numbers.
explanations.art: A line graph shaped like a lazy S, with hours along the bottom and the running total of sprouted seeds up the side, and the middle point marked.

explanations.concept: Why it helps seeds to wake at different times
explanations.description: Weather is hard to predict. A first rain may be followed by weeks of dry heat. If every seed woke at that first rain, a dry spell could kill every seedling and the plant would leave no young at all. If seeds wake over several days, or over several rains, some are sure to be in the ground at a good time. Biologists call this spreading the risk, or bet hedging. In 1966, an Israeli scientist, Dan Cohen, worked out with mathematics that in a place where rain is unpredictable, a plant does better when only some of their seeds wake in any one year. Many desert plants do exactly this. Part of the story is not settled. Some of the spread may be a plan the plant made over many generations. Some may simply be small differences that nobody needed to plan.
examples: Wildflowers in dry places keep a store of sleeping seeds in the soil, and wake only a part of them after each rain.
A farmer sows bajra in many lots over the rainy season, so that a dry spell cannot spoil every lot. This is the same idea, used by a person.
Weeds in a field come up all season long, even after the field was ploughed, because their seeds wake a few at a time.
explanations.art: A desert field after a light rain, with a few seedlings up, many seeds still sleeping in the soil, and a thundercloud far away.

perspectives.explanation: The spread in wake-up times is a result of natural selection. Plants whose seeds all woke at once sometimes lost everything, so plants that spread the risk left more young over many years.
A part of the spread is just the small, unplanned differences between seeds, and has no job to do. It is hard to tell which part is a plan and which part is chance.

explanations.concept: Dormancy: alive, wet, warm, and still asleep
explanations.definition: Dormancy is when a living seed does not sprout even though the seed has water, warmth and air. Dormancy stops a seed from waking at a bad time.
explanations.description: Moong has almost no dormancy, which is why moong sprouts so quickly. Many wild seeds are different. If a seed woke at the first warm day of autumn, the cold winter would kill the seedling. So the seed waits for a sign that winter has passed. Seed scientists describe two main kinds of dormancy. In one kind, the seed coat is the problem. It is so hard, or so waxy, that water cannot get in. In the other kind, the baby plant inside is held back by chemical signals until the right sign arrives. Dormancy is not damage and it is not death. A dormant seed is doing exactly the job that seeds are made for, which is to wait for the right time.
examples: A tamarind seed has a coat so hard that water hardly gets in, even after a night of soaking.
An apple seed has water and air in the fridge, but wakes properly only after weeks of cold.
Moong, chana and rajma have very little dormancy. They wake within a day or two of getting wet.
explanations.art: A seed in damp soil with a closed padlock on the seed coat, beside a seed with an open padlock and a root coming out.

explanations.concept: The keys that unlock a sleeping seed
explanations.definition: Different seeds wait for different signs. The sign might be a thin spot in the coat, a spell of cold, a flash of light, smoke from a fire, or a big rain. A sign that wakes a seed is like a key.
explanations.description: A hard coat can be thinned by sandpaper, by slowly rotting in the soil, or by passing through the gut of a bird or a bat. A spell of cold tells apple seeds that winter is over. Light tells tiny seeds that they are near the surface, so their small food store will last until the shoot reaches the sun. Smoke tells some Australian and South African seeds that a fire has just cleared the land and given them room. A big rain tells some desert wildflower seeds that the soil is wet deep down. In the 1940s, a plant scientist called Frits Went suggested that seeds of some desert wildflowers have a chemical in the coat that only a large rain washes away. A small shower wets the soil for only a day or two. It does not wash the chemical away, so the seeds stay asleep. The keys are all different. But each one is a sign that tells the seed that a good time has come.
examples: Tamarind: a rough rub thins the coat, so water can get in.
Apple: weeks of cold tell the seed that winter has passed.
Some desert wildflowers: a big rain washes away the sleep chemical.
explanations.art: Six keys on a ring, each labelled with a sign: rub, cold, light, smoke, big rain and bird gut, next to six different seeds.

explanations.concept: Two messengers inside a seed: sleep and wake
explanations.description: Inside a seed, two plant hormones pull in opposite directions. Abscisic acid tells the seed to stay asleep. Gibberellin tells the seed to wake. A seed wakes when the balance tips from sleep to wake. In seeds that need a cold chill, the cold slowly lowers the sleep messenger and raises the wake messenger. In barley, the baby plant makes gibberellin, which travels to the food store and tells it to start making enzymes, the helpers that cut starch into sugar. Seed scientists have worked out many of the steps. How a seed adds up all the signs of water, warmth, light and cold, and tips the balance at just the right moment, is still being studied.
examples: A seed that makes more of the sleep messenger stays asleep longer.
When a barley grain wakes, the gibberellin goes from the baby plant to the food store, and the food store starts to work.
Gardeners sometimes soak stubborn seeds in a weak gibberellin solution, because it works as a wake message.
explanations.art: A balance scale with a 'sleep' hormone weight on one pan and a 'wake' hormone weight on the other, with a seed on top.

perspectives.explanation: The balance of the two messengers is the main switch. It is a chemical sum, and the seed's own chemistry does it.
The seed is deciding. The seed senses many signs, remembers the cold, and acts at the right time. These biologists say this counts as a simple kind of thinking without a brain.

explanations.concept: How deep can a seed be sown? The food store sets the limit
explanations.definition: A shoot has to push up through the soil before the shoot can see light. The shoot lives on the food in the seed all that time. So the bigger the seed's food store, the deeper the seed can be sown.
explanations.description: A tiny mustard seed has only a pinch of food. If the seed is buried 6 centimetres deep, the baby plant grows a pale, thin shoot and uses up the food before reaching the surface. The seedling dies in the dark, still under the soil. A big chana has a large food store, and the shoot can climb 6 centimetres or more and still have food to spare. Gardeners use a rule of thumb. Sow a seed about two or three times as deep as the seed is wide. A shoot grows in the dark by stretching, and stretching spends food fast. That is why a tiny seed that is buried deep fails. This is also why tiny seeds such as some lettuce wait for light before waking. The light tells them that they are near the surface.
examples: A mustard seed is about 1 millimetre wide, so the seed is sown about 1 centimetre deep.
A chana is about 8 millimetres wide, so the chana can be sown 3 to 5 centimetres deep.
A coconut, one of the biggest seeds, is often planted lying half-buried because the seed has so much food.
explanations.art: A cutaway of soil with a tiny mustard seed sown deep with a thin pale shoot that stops, and a large chana sown deep whose shoot reaches the light.

explanations.concept: Big food store or tiny food store: two ways to bet
explanations.definition: A plant can make a few big seeds with a lot of food each, or a huge number of tiny seeds with little food each. Both ways work, and each has a price.
explanations.description: A mango tree makes a few big stones with plenty of food, so each young tree has a good start. The price is that the tree can make only a few. A banyan or a peepal makes huge numbers of tiny seeds, each with very little food. The price is that nearly every seed fails. The orchid is the most extreme. An orchid seed is as fine as dust and has almost no food store at all. In the wild, an orchid seed can only grow when a tiny fungus in the soil feeds the seed. The largest seed in the world is the coco de mer of the Seychelles islands, which can weigh more than 10 kilograms. The seed grows very slowly, and the tree is slow to make seeds. Neither way is better. They are two different bets on a hard world.
examples: Mango and coconut: a few big seeds, each with a large store of food.
Banyan and peepal: thousands of tiny seeds, each with a tiny store of food.
Orchids: dust-like seeds with almost no food, fed by a fungus in the soil.
explanations.art: A mango stone at the front of a tray, a small pile of banyan seeds, and a pinch of orchid dust, with a note on food stores.

explanations.concept: Two ways a seedling comes up
explanations.definition: Some seedlings pull their seed leaves up into the air, where the leaves turn green. This is epigeal germination. Others leave the seed leaves under the soil and send up only the shoot. This is hypogeal germination.
explanations.description: In moong and rajma, the stem just below the seed leaves, called the hypocotyl, bends into a hook. The hook pulls the fat seed leaves up out of the soil. In the light, they turn green and work like small leaves for a while. In chana and peas, the part of the stem above the seed leaves does the growing. It pushes up through the soil, and the seed leaves stay under the ground, still feeding the seedling. Grasses such as rice, wheat and maize are different again. A sheath, called the coleoptile, covers the first leaf like a sharp tip and pushes through the soil. A seed leaf under the soil is protected from being eaten and from drying out. A seed leaf in the air gets light and can make some food.
examples: Moong and rajma: seed leaves lifted into the light and turned green.
Chana and peas: seed leaves stay under the soil.
Rice, wheat and maize: a pointed sheath pushes up, and the first leaf follows inside it.
explanations.art: Three seedlings in cutaway soil: moong with seed leaves in the air, chana with seed leaves buried, and rice with a pointed sheath.

explanations.concept: The pale search: a seedling that cannot find light
explanations.definition: A seedling grown in the dark stretches fast, stays pale and thin, and keeps the tiny leaves folded. The seedling is searching for light and spending their food to do it. Scientists call this an etiolated seedling.
explanations.description: In the dark, a seedling puts nearly everything into growing longer. Their stem grows long and thin, their leaves stay small and folded, and the hook at the top stays closed. They make almost no chlorophyll, the green substance that catches sunlight, so they are pale yellow or white. The long stem is the best use of their food. The sooner the top reaches the surface, the sooner they can make new food. Bean sprouts are sold long and white because they are grown in the dark on purpose. If the seedling reaches light, things change within hours. The stem slows down, the hook opens, the leaves unfold and chlorophyll starts to form, so they turn green. If they do not reach light before the food runs out, they cannot recover.
examples: Moong grown in a dark box for five days is long, thin and pale.
The same moong in a bright window is shorter, thicker and green, with open leaves.
A potato in a dark cupboard sends out long, pale shoots that search for light.
explanations.art: Two rows of moong seedlings: a dark box with tall pale thin ones, and a window with short green sturdy ones.

explanations.concept: Light flips the switch: how a seedling knows she has reached the sun
explanations.description: A seedling has light sensors, which are proteins that change shape when light hits them. The first ones found were called phytochromes, which sense red and far-red light. Others sense blue light. When a sensor catches light, it sends a message that changes which genes are switched on. The stem slows down, the leaves open and the cells start to make chlorophyll. Scientists have found many of the proteins and genes in this chain. A seedling cannot see the way we do, and they have no eyes. Yet they tell the difference between dark, shade and bright sun, and tell the direction the light comes from. How the seedling's cells combine all these messages is still being worked out.
examples: A moong seedling moved from a dark box to a window starts to turn green the same day.
A seedling under the shade of a bigger plant stretches taller, as if she senses the shade.
A seedling in a window leans towards the glass.
explanations.art: A pale seedling on one side and a green seedling on the other, with a dotted arrow showing a light sensor sending a message to the leaves.

perspectives.explanation: A seedling has sensors and chemical switches that respond to light. The pale search is a built-in programme, and light turns off the pale search programme and turns on the green programme.
A seedling senses shade, light and direction, and then changes how they grow. These scientists say that this is making a choice. They call it a simple kind of thinking, done by cells without a brain.

explanations.concept: How seeds keep for years: dry and cold slow the ageing
explanations.definition: Seeds slowly age and get damaged inside, even when they are asleep. Dry and cold slow the damage. A drier, colder seed lives longer.
explanations.description: A sleeping seed still uses a tiny bit of food and slowly wears out. Water is what drives the wearing out, so a very dry seed lasts longer. Warmth speeds it up, so a cold seed lasts longer too. An American seed scientist, James Harrington, wrote down two rough rules of thumb. For each 1 percent less water in a seed, the seed lives about twice as long. For each 5 degrees Celsius or so colder, the seed lives about twice as long. These rules only work within limits, but they show why seed banks dry their seeds and freeze them. India's national seed bank in New Delhi keeps crop seeds in very cold rooms at around minus 20 degrees Celsius. At home, a monsoon kitchen is bad for seeds, because the air is damp and warm. A tightly closed jar with a spoon of dry rice or a silica packet inside keeps the seeds much drier.
examples: A sealed jar of dry chana in a cool cupboard keeps the seeds sprouting for years.
The same chana in an open bowl in a monsoon kitchen can mould, or sprout too early.
Seed banks freeze seeds because every drop of 5 degrees Celsius roughly doubles the time that the seed stays alive.
explanations.art: A jar of seeds on a kitchen shelf in the monsoon with damp air, next to a sealed jar in a cold seed bank room with frost on the shelf.

explanations.concept: Seeds that cannot wait: mango, jackfruit and cocoa
explanations.definition: Some seeds die if they dry out. They must be sown fresh while still wet. They cannot be kept in a dry seed bank. Scientists call them wet-keeping, or recalcitrant, seeds.
explanations.description: Moong, chana and rice are dry-keeping seeds. They finish growing, dry out on purpose, and then wait. Mango, jackfruit, cocoa and many trees of wet forests are different. Their seeds never dry out inside the fruit and have no sleeping stage. They sprout soon after the fruit falls, if the ground is damp. Neem seeds are known to lose their power to sprout within a few weeks. Seed banks cannot store these seeds in the usual way. This is a real problem, because many trees of wet forests have wet-keeping seeds. Scientists are testing new ways to keep them, such as cutting out only the tiny baby plant and freezing the baby plant in very cold liquid nitrogen. Nobody yet has a way that works for every kind.
examples: A mango stone left in a dry drawer for a few months will not sprout. A fresh stone in damp soil sprouts in a few weeks.
Jackfruit seeds sprout best when sown within days of eating the fruit.
Cocoa seeds begin to sprout inside the pod if the pod is left too long.
explanations.art: A mango stone in damp soil with a sprout, and next to the stone a dried-out stone in a drawer with a cross.

explanations.concept: Do seeds remember? Seed priming and the mother's weather
explanations.description: Seed scientists find that the behaviour of a seed depends on the past. Seeds that were soaked a little, then dried again, often wake faster when they are soaked the second time. Farmers and seed companies use this trick, which is called priming. Seeds from a plant that grew in a cold summer may be more dormant than seeds from the same kind of plant grown in a hot summer. So a seed carries something from their mother plant's weather. Scientists are studying how this happens. One idea is that chemical marks on the genes change how they switch on and off. But does carrying marks from the past count as remembering? The question depends on what we mean by the word.
examples: Farmers in some places soak seed overnight and dry the seed in the shade before sowing, so that the plants come up faster.
Seeds from a plant that grew in a cool summer can stay dormant longer than seeds from a plant that grew in a hot summer.
explanations.art: A seed with a thin trail of tiny marks leading back to a mother plant standing in rain and cold.

perspectives.explanation: Priming and the mother's weather are chemical changes that last. They are a kind of memory in a loose sense, but they are not the same as a brain remembering.
Any living thing that keeps a trace of the past and uses it later is remembering. A seed that is primed or marked by their mother plant's weather remembers in their own way.

agreed.text: Seeds from one batch wake at different times, even when they get exactly the same conditions.
agreed.evidence: Seed labs and farmers have counted germination day by day for more than a century. The running total always rises in a lazy S shape, with some seeds early and some late.

agreed.text: The germination percentage of a batch of seeds can be measured, and a bigger sample gives a steadier answer.
agreed.evidence: Labs compare many lots of 100 seeds. Small tests with 10 seeds vary a lot from lot to lot, while tests of 100 or 400 seeds agree much better.

agreed.text: A seed with a bigger food store can be sown deeper than a seed with a smaller store.
agreed.evidence: Sowing depth tests with many crops show that large seeds come up from deeper soil than small seeds, and tiny seeds fail when they are sown too deep.

agreed.text: Many seeds are dormant, and need a particular sign such as a thinned coat, a spell of cold, light, smoke or a big rain before they wake.
agreed.evidence: Growers have used these keys for generations, and seed scientists have tested them in laboratories on thousands of kinds of seed.

agreed.text: A seedling grown without light is long, thin and pale. Light changes their growth within hours.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can see it by growing bean sprouts in the dark and in the light. Plant scientists have found the light sensors that cause the change.

agreed.text: Seeds live longer when they are drier and colder, but some seeds, such as mango and jackfruit, die if they dry out.
agreed.evidence: Seed banks measure how long seeds survive in storage. Seeds of wet forest trees are killed by the drying that keeps dry-keeping seeds alive.

challenging.claim: A seed that has not sprouted when the others have is dead.
challenging.who: Many gardeners, and many people checking a plate of seeds.
challenging.for: Most live seeds sprout within a day or two on a plate. A seed with no root after a long time looks like a dud.
challenging.against: Seeds from one batch wake over days and sometimes weeks. In 1859, Charles Darwin kept three spoonfuls of pond mud covered in his study. He counted 537 plants that rose from it over six months, and many seeds must have waited a long time. A late seed is often alive and only slow.

challenging.claim: The seeds that wake first are the strongest, and the late ones are weak.
challenging.who: Some farmers and some seed testers.
challenging.for: In tests of seed vigour, seeds that sprout fast often grow into bigger seedlings.
challenging.against: In a dry year, the early seedlings may all die and the late ones may be the only survivors. Fast and slow seeds are each good in different weather. Strong or weak depends on the year.

challenging.claim: The deeper you sow a seed, the safer the seed is.
challenging.for: Deep soil is cooler and wetter, and birds and ants cannot find seeds easily.
challenging.against: A small seed has only a small food store. If the seed is buried too deep, the shoot uses up the food before the shoot reaches the light. A seed should be sown about two or three times as deep as the seed is wide.

challenging.claim: Soaking any seed in very hot water makes the seed sprout faster.
challenging.for: A brief dip in hot water helps some very hard seeds, such as some acacia seeds, by cracking the coat.
challenging.against: Hot water cooks the baby plant inside most seeds, and a cooked seed never sprouts. Most seeds, including moong and chana, only need ordinary water. Hot water is risky for children as well.

challenging.claim: Old local varieties of seeds are always better than new ones.
challenging.who: Some farmers, seed savers and food writers.
challenging.for: Old local varieties have been grown in the same place for generations. They often cope well with local weather and pests, and they add variety that protects against disease.
challenging.against: Some new varieties give much bigger harvests or resist particular diseases. Many farmers use both. Variety is the key point, and nobody knows in advance which kind will cope best with next year's weather.

big_questions.q: If every seed in a packet woke in the same hour, what could go wrong? And what does that tell you about why they do not?
big_questions.hint: Think about a first rain that is followed by three weeks of heat.

big_questions.q: A tiny seed does not know how deep they are buried. So how can the seed wake only when they are near the top?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the soil near the top has that the soil far down does not.

big_questions.q: A seed in a vault is alive but waiting for 100 years. Is waiting a way of being alive, or a way of being paused?
big_questions.hint: Is a person asleep alive in the same way as a person running?

big_questions.q: Is the germination percentage on a packet a fact about the seeds, or a fact about the test?
big_questions.hint: Would a different lot of seeds, or a different room, give the same number?

big_questions.q: Farmers have saved and swapped seeds for about ten thousand years, and nobody can name the people who first grew rice or wheat. Who do seeds belong to?
big_questions.hint: Who made the first rice? How many people helped, over how many years?

big_questions.q: In some years, rain turns a dry desert into a carpet of flowers. The seeds waited for years for that rain. What does a seed's waiting say about time?
big_questions.hint: How long can you wait for something you really want?

big_questions.q: Seeds that wake late can save the whole group in a bad year. Should we call a slow one weak or smart?
big_questions.hint: In which kind of year is the slow seed the lucky one?

big_questions.q: Plant scientists argue about whether a seed that adds up signs of cold, light and water is deciding. What would you need to see before you said a seed decides?
big_questions.hint: What does it mean when you decide something? What do you do differently?

story.title: The Second Rain
story.note: Hema, her family and their village are made up. The science is real. Bajra is a main crop in the Thar desert, farmers there sow it with the first rain, and a dry spell after a light first rain can kill the seedlings. Seeds in dry sand stay asleep until enough rain reaches them. The numbers in Hema's count are made up, but the shape is typical.
text: Hema lived in a small village in the Thar desert, not far from Jaisalmer. Her house was made of mud and stone, and the sand around it went on in waves as far as she could see. Rain was rare there. Dadi, her grandmother, said that rain was like a guest who comes when she likes, and never says when.

Every family kept its seed for the next year in a clay pot with a mud lid. Dadi's pot held bajra, the grain that grows best in the desert. All year, the pot stood in the coolest corner of the house, and Hema was not allowed to touch it.

At school, Sunita Madam gave the class some homework. 'Put thirty seeds on a wet cloth,' she said. 'Count how many have a root after twelve hours, after twenty-four hours, after thirty-six, and so on. Write the numbers down.' Hema asked Dadi for thirty seeds from the pot. Dadi gave her a long look, and then thirty seeds.

Hema counted. After twelve hours, six seeds had a tiny white tail. After twenty-four hours, seventeen. After thirty-six, twenty-five. After two days, twenty-seven. One more woke on the third day, and one more on the sixth. One seed never woke at all. 'They had the same cloth and the same water,' Hema told the cat. 'Why did they not wake together?' The cat did not know.

Then, one evening, the smell came. Wet sand smells like nothing else in the world. Clouds had rolled over the dunes, and rain fell for an hour. The whole village came out and stood in it with their faces up. In the morning, Hema's uncle, Bhanwar Chacha, took Dadi's pot to the field. He scattered the seeds along the rows and covered them with sand, the way he did every year. 'Sow at the first rain,' he said, 'and the crop gets the longest season.'

Four days later, the whole field was striped with thin green blades. The neighbours laughed for joy. Then the clouds went away, and the hot wind came back. One day passed. Then five. Then ten. The sand dried out to the depth of a hand. The green blades turned yellow, then brown, and then they fell over.

Bhanwar Chacha stood at the edge of the field with his turban in his hand. 'The seed was no good,' he said. 'Or the rain was a trick. We have lost the whole crop.' He began to talk about borrowing money to buy new seed and sow again.

Hema went into the field and knelt beside a row of dead blades. She thought of her cloth and her counts. Six seeds first. Twenty-five by the second day. And the last ones, long after the others. Not every seed in the pot had woken on the same day. So why should the seeds in the field be different? The rain had wetted only the top of the sand. Perhaps only some seeds had met the water.

She dug into the sand with her fingers, just below a dead blade. There, she found a plump, hard bajra seed. She pressed her nail into the seed. Inside, the baby plant was pale and firm. The seed was alive. She dug again, ten steps along, and found another. And another.

'Chacha,' she said, 'do not buy new seed. The field is not empty. Many of the seeds are still asleep.' He laughed, but not unkindly. 'A plate of seeds is not a field, beti.' 'It is the same pot,' said Hema. 'On my cloth, six seeds woke first and one woke last of all. Same seeds, same water, and no two woke together. They are just different from each other.'

Bhanwar Chacha was quiet for a long time. He looked at Hema, and then at Dadi. Dadi lifted one shoulder, the way she did when she was not going to say what she thought. 'It costs nothing to wait a week,' she said. Chacha put his turban back on.

Five days later, the second rain came. This one was a big one, and it fell all night. Hema lay awake and listened to it drum on the roof. In the morning, the sand was dark and wet down to a man's elbow.

Three days after that, new blades began to push out of the wet sand, between the dead brown ones. There were a few at first, then more, then more. 'Late seeds,' Hema told the cat. The cat looked unimpressed.
The field never looked as full as it would have if the first rain had been kind. But it carried a crop. In the cold months, there was bajra in Dadi's pot again, and bajra rotis on every plate.

After that year, Bhanwar Chacha always held back a third of the seed for a second sowing, in case the first rain was a trick. He asked Hema to count each new lot on a wet cloth. 'Tell me when the last one wakes,' he said. 'I want to know how long to wait.' Hema wrote the numbers in a notebook with a green cover. The first column and the last column were far apart. She had begun to think that this was not an accident.
story.epiphany: Seeds from one pot do not wake together. After a false start, the seeds that were still asleep can save the crop.
ask: Why did the seedlings that sprouted after the first rain die, while many seeds in the sand stayed alive?
On Hema's cloth, the seeds woke at different times. What did that tell her about the seeds in the field?
Why might a farmer hold back a third of the seed for a second sowing?
Chacha said that a plate of seeds is not a field. How could you check whether a plate test tells you the truth about a field?
Hema pressed a nail into a seed to see if the baby plant was alive. What else could you do to find out if a waiting seed is alive?

games.title: Wake or Wait: choose when your seeds wake
games.context: This is a card game about timing. Each round shows a sign in the weather. You decide how many of your seeds to wake. If the weather turns out good, they grow. If it turns bad, they are lost.

setup.art: Six dry moong seeds in a row on a paper mat with three spaces labelled SLEEPING, GROWING and LOST.

setup.caption: 2. Turn over the top card and read only the SIGN side.

setup.art: A player holding two seeds in a closed fist while the reader holds the card with the back facing the players.
setup.caption: 3. Choose secretly how many seeds to wake. Hold them in your fist. Then the back is read.

printables.title: A mat for each player with three spaces: SLEEPING, GROWING and LOST
items: Mat: three boxes in a row, labelled SLEEPING, GROWING (2 points for each seed) and LOST (0 points). Each player puts six dry seeds on SLEEPING at the start.

printables.title: A score sheet with a row for each round
items: Round | Seeds I woke | Safe or danger? | Points I earned
Total at the end: points from GROWING, plus 1 point for each seed still on SLEEPING

rules: Each player takes six dry seeds, such as moong or chana, and puts them on the SLEEPING box of their mat.
Shuffle the 24 cards and put them face down. You will play 12 rounds, so you use 12 cards.
In each round, the reader turns over the top card and reads only the front, which is the sign. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Every player secretly picks 0, 1, 2 or 3 sleeping seeds to wake, and holds them in a closed fist. Nobody may wake more than 3 in a round.

The reader reads the back. If it says SAFE, every woken seed grows. Move the seed to GROWING. Each one is worth 2 points. If it says DANGER, every woken seed is lost. Move the seed to LOST. Each one is worth 0 points.
Seeds that stayed asleep are safe. The job of reader passes to the next player after each round.
After 12 rounds, each seed still on SLEEPING is worth 1 point, because the seed can still wake another year. The player with the most points wins, and ties share the win.
Playing alone: play against the cards, with a score sheet. Try to score 8 or more. Then play again with a different plan, and see if your score changes.

flow.context: This is the first step of Wake or Wait. You set up the mats, the seeds and the cards.
flow.do: 1. Give each player a mat and six seeds. 2. Shuffle the cards and put them face down. 3. Choose the first reader.
flow.say: In this game you are seeds in a field. Each round shows a sign about the weather. You choose how many seeds to wake. A good rain makes them grow. A bad spell loses them.
flow.kid: Put six seeds on your mat. The cards are the weather. You choose when to wake.
flow.parent: Seeds are small, so keep them away from toddlers and out of mouths. No printer? Write each card on a small slip of paper. With one child and a parent, both play and take turns as reader. Playing alone, turn the card so only the sign shows, write your choice, then turn it over.

flow.context: In this step you play one practice round to learn how the game works.
flow.do: Play one practice round. The reader turns over a card and reads only the sign. Each player picks a number of seeds, then the reader reads the back.
flow.say: The sign is only a clue. It may be a good clue or a trick. How many seeds will you wake? Why that many?
flow.kid: Read the sign. Wake 0, 1, 2 or 3 seeds. Say why.

ask.q: Why would you wake only some of your seeds, not all of them at once?
good: If the weather turns bad, I lose them all.
I want to keep some seeds safe.
A sign is only a clue, so it can be wrong.

flow.parent: Let your child say the reason before the back is read. Do not tell them what to do. Children usually wake three seeds on the first round, and then become more careful. That change is the lesson.

flow.context: In this step you play the first half of the game.
flow.do: Play rounds 2 to 6. After each round, move the seeds on the mats. Keep a tally of points on the score sheet.
flow.say: Look at the sign. Make your choice in secret. Then we see what the weather did. Keep going.
flow.kid: Play five more rounds. Keep your fist closed until the card is read.

check.q: A player wakes all three allowed seeds on a round with a poor sign. The back says DANGER. What happens?
options: The seeds go back to sleep
check.why: Every woken seed is lost in a dangerous spell. A seed that woke cannot go back to sleep. A seed that stayed asleep is safe. That is why waking only some seeds is a safer plan.

flow.context: In this step you finish the game and count the scores.
flow.do: Play rounds 7 to 12. Count the seeds on SLEEPING, GROWING and LOST. Work out the scores.
flow.say: Keep going. Count your points after the last round. Seeds still asleep count one point each.
flow.kid: Play the last six rounds. Then count your points.
flow.parent: A seed still asleep at the end is worth 1 point. A growing plant is worth 2. A lost seed is worth 0. Check each player's total before talking.

flow.context: In this step you talk about what the game showed.
flow.do: Look at who scored the most. Ask the questions below. Then ask what a plant might gain if only some of their seeds wake each year.
flow.say: Who won? Did the player who woke the most seeds win? What did the winner do differently?
flow.kid: Who won? Did the winner wake the most seeds? Talk about what they did.

ask.q: What did the winner do that the others did not?
good: They woke some seeds and kept some asleep.
They waited for good signs.
They did not wake everything at once.

flow.think: A real plant cannot read a sign card. How could a plant spread their seeds over time without reading signs?

check.q: In the game, a player who woke all her seeds as early as possible usually did badly. Why?
options: One bad spell of weather lost all her seeds
Seeds do not grow in good weather
Waking seeds early is against the rules
check.why: If every seed wakes together, one bad day can destroy every one of them. A player who spreads out her choices keeps some seeds safe. Real seeds in a desert do much the same thing.

games.title: Wake-Up Keys: match each seed to the key that wakes them
games.context: This is a memory game. Every sleeping seed waits for a different sign, or key. Players turn over cards to match each seed with the key that wakes the seed.

setup.art: A child turning over two cards, a tamarind seed card and a rough-rub key card.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over two cards. If a seed card and the matching key card go together, keep them.

setup.caption: 3. Say why each pair matches. The player with the most pairs wins.

printables.title: A score sheet for pairs and turns
items: Player | Pairs found | Turns taken (for playing alone) | My best number of turns so far

rules: Cut out the 20 cards. Shuffle them and lay them face down in four rows of five.
On your turn, turn over any two cards and show them to everyone.
If one is a seed and the other is the key that wakes that seed, you keep both. Say in one sentence why they go together. Then take another turn.
If they do not match, turn both cards face down again in the same places. The next player has a turn.
Two seed cards, or two key cards, never match.
When all the cards are taken, the player with the most pairs wins. Ties share the win.
Playing alone: count how many turns you need to find all ten pairs. Write it on the score sheet. Next time, try to beat it.

flow.context: This is the first step of Wake-Up Keys. You read the cards, then set them out.
flow.do: Look through all 20 cards face up together for two minutes. Then shuffle them and lay them face down in four rows of five.
flow.say: Every seed waits for a key. Some keys are rubs or cold. Some are rain. Let's read the cards first, then play.
flow.kid: Read all 20 cards. Then mix them and lay them face down.
flow.parent: No printer? Write each of the 20 lines on a small slip of paper. Two to four players take turns. One child plays alone and counts turns. Before the first game, let your child guess three matches out loud.

flow.context: In this step you practise one pair before the game starts.
flow.do: Do one practice pair. Pick the tamarind seed and the matching key together. Read both cards aloud.
flow.say: The tamarind seed has a coat so hard that water hardly gets in. What key would help the seed? Why?
flow.kid: Find the tamarind seed card. Which key helps the seed? Say why.

ask.q: Why would a rough rub help a tamarind seed?
good: It thins the hard coat.
It lets water get in.
The baby plant inside cannot drink until water can get in.

flow.parent: A rub thins the coat, so water can soak in and the seed swells. The same job is done in nature by time, by the acids in an animal's gut, or by the soil.

flow.context: In this step you play the memory game.
flow.do: Play by the rules. Each time a player finds a pair, they say in one sentence why the seed and the key go together.
flow.say: Turn over two cards. A seed and the matching key? Keep them and tell us why they match.
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. Find a seed and the matching key. Say why they match.

check.q: Which key helps a desert wildflower seed that has a sleep chemical in the coat?
options: A big rain that washes the chemical away
check.why: A small shower would not wash away the chemical, so the seed stays asleep. A big rain tells the seed that the soil is wet deep down, and a seedling can grow.

flow.context: In this step you sort the keys into groups to see what they have in common.
flow.do: Lay the ten pairs in a row. Ask your child to sort the keys into three groups. The three groups are: water, time or cold, and other living things.
flow.say: Look at all ten keys. Which ones are about water? Which are about time or cold? Which depend on other living things?
flow.kid: Sort the ten keys into three groups: water, time or cold, and other living things.
flow.parent: There is no single right sort. Rain, the bird's gut and the rub can all be seen as ways of letting in water. Accept any group a child can explain.
flow.think: Different seeds wait for different keys. Is waiting for a key the same as being asleep?

items.p: You test 30 seeds from a packet on a wet cloth. After four days, 24 of them have a root. What is the germination percentage?
items.why: 24 out of 30 is the same as 8 out of 10, which is 80 out of every 100, or 80 percent. Picking 24 percent means using the count itself as the percentage, which only works when exactly 100 seeds are tested.

items.p: You count the seeds with a root on a plate. You find 4 at 12 hours, 15 at 24 hours and 24 at 36 hours. How many new seeds woke between 24 hours and 36 hours? ____
items.why: 24 take away 15 is 9. The counts are running totals, so the new seeds in each period are found by taking one count away from the next.

items.p: Put 30 seeds from one packet on each of two plates in the same room. The two plates will give exactly the same count at every hour.
items.why: False. Even identical-looking plates differ a little, because each seed is a little different. A small difference between two plates is normal, and a good reason to test with more seeds.

items.p: Why do the seeds in one packet not all wake at the same hour?
opts: Each seed is a little different, so water and warmth reach each baby plant at a different speed
The seeds argue about who goes first
Only the biggest seeds can wake
items.why: No two seeds are exactly alike. One has a thinner coat, one is a little bigger, one sat in a different part of the pod. These small differences spread the wake-up times out. Picking 'only the biggest' is a common guess, but small seeds wake too.

items.p: Describe in two or three sentences what the waking curve of a plate of seeds looks like, and what it shows about the seeds.
items.a: The line starts slowly, climbs steeply in the middle and goes flat at the end, like a lazy S. It shows that a few seeds wake early, most wake in the middle and a few wake late. Seeds from one packet do not wake together.
items.why: A strong answer describes the shape and then says what the shape means about the seeds.

items.p: Match each sleeping seed to the sign that helps the seed wake.
pairs: a rough rub that thins the coat
items.why: Each seed waits for the sign that tells the seed that a good time has come. A hard coat needs thinning. An apple seed needs winter to pass. A desert seed needs a rain big enough to wet the soil deep down. A bush seed senses that a fire has cleared the land. A tiny seed senses that they are near the surface.

items.p: A seed is alive, and has water, warmth and air, but still does not sprout. What is this called?
items.why: Dormancy is when a living seed holds back, even though conditions seem right, until the right sign comes. Germination is the opposite, when the seed starts to grow. Picking 'dead' would be wrong, because a dormant seed is alive.

items.p: A tiny mustard seed is sown 8 centimetres deep. A big chana is sown 8 centimetres deep too. Which is more likely to reach the top, and why?
opts: The chana, because the bigger food store can feed a long climb in the dark
The mustard, because the seed is lighter
Both reach the top, because shoots always find the light
Neither, because seeds cannot grow in soil
items.why: A shoot grows in the dark using the food in the seed. The chana has a big food store, so the shoot can travel a long way. The mustard seed has only a pinch of food and runs out first. Picking 'lighter' mixes up weight with food store.

items.p: A gardener's rule says to sow a seed about two or three times as deep as the seed is wide. Explain in your own words why.
items.a: A seed has to push a shoot up through the soil using the food stored inside, because there is no light underground. A deeper sowing means a longer climb. A bigger seed has more food and can climb further. The rule matches the depth to the amount of food, so the shoot arrives at the surface before the food runs out.
items.why: A strong answer links the depth to the food store and says that the shoot lives on that food until it reaches the light.

items.p: Which of these seeds is the odd one out? Moong, chana, rice, mango stone.
items.why: Moong, chana and rice are dry-keeping seeds. They finish growing, dry out and can wait for years. A mango stone is a wet-keeping seed, which dies on drying out and must be sown fresh.

items.p: Put these in order, from first to last, as a moong seedling comes up from the soil.
items: The seed drinks water and swells
The first root comes out and grows down
The stem bends into a hook and pulls the seed leaves up through the soil
The hook straightens and the seed leaves open in the light
items.why: First the seed drinks and swells. The root comes out first and anchors the seedling. Then the stem forms a hook and pulls the fat seed leaves up out of the soil. In the light, the hook straightens and the leaves open.
