peas
Seed leaves stay under the soil
items.why: In moong and rajma, the stem hooks and pulls the fat seed leaves up into the light. In chana and peas, the stem above the seed leaves does the growing, and the seed leaves stay in the soil.

items.p: Bean sprouts from the market are long and white. Why are they grown in the dark?
opts: In the dark the sprouts stretch long and stay pale, which is what people want to eat
They grow slower in the dark
items.why: A seedling in the dark stretches fast and makes almost no chlorophyll, so they stay pale. Growers use this on purpose. Picking 'light would kill the seeds' is wrong, because the same seeds grow well in light as green, shorter seedlings.

items.p: A pale seedling that has grown in a dark box begins to turn green within a day or two of being moved to a window.
items.why: True. Light switches on the making of chlorophyll, the green substance that catches sunlight. The tips usually start to turn greener within a day, and the leaves begin to open.

items.p: You are counting seeds on a plate. After four days, three seeds still have no root. Three friends give you advice.

views.says: They are dead. Throw them away and write down that 27 out of 30 woke.
Wait two more days, because a late seed is often only slow.
Press each one with a nail. A seed that is firm and plump may still be alive.

items.ask: Which advice would you follow? Give a reason from what you know about seeds. Then say one thing that another friend gets right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the idea that seeds in one batch wake at different times. Farhan's advice fits that idea best: seeds can be late. Lakshmi's test is a useful check that does not wait. Nisha is right that some seeds really are dead, but she cannot know that yet. A strong answer picks one and gives the others their due.
items.why: Seeds that wake late are common, and a firm, plump seed may still be alive. But some seeds really are dead. The best plan combines waiting with a check.

items.p: Draw a waking curve for a plate of 30 seeds. Put the hours along the bottom and the number of seeds with a root up the side. Show a lazy S shape, and mark where about half the seeds had woken.
items.a: A line graph with hours along the bottom and seeds with a root up the side. The line starts low, climbs steeply in the middle and flattens near the top. A mark is on the line where it reaches about 15 seeds.
items.why: The shape shows that seeds wake at different times, with a few early, most in the middle and a few late.
items.art: An empty graph with labelled axes, hours across and number of seeds up.

items.p: A packet says that 80 percent of its seeds sprout. You want 40 plants. How many seeds should you sow? ____
items.why: 80 percent means 8 of every 10 seeds sprout. 40 plants is 5 lots of 8, so you need 5 lots of 10 seeds, which is 50 seeds. Sowing only 40 would give about 32 plants.

items.p: In a desert, the first rain of the year is often light, and a long dry spell may follow. Which sowing plan is the safest for a farmer?
opts: Sow all the seed at the first rain
Sow part of the seed at the first rain and keep part for a later rain
Sow nothing until the end of the rainy season
Sow the seed in the hottest week
items.why: A farmer who sows in two lots is spreading the risk. If the first lot is lost in a dry spell, the second lot may survive. Seeds that wake at different times work in the same way. Picking 'all the seed at the first rain' risks losing everything.

items.p: A farmer says that the seeds that did not come up after the first rain are dead. Plan a fair test to find out. What will you do, and what will you look for?
items.a: Dig up several seeds that did not come up. Press them with a nail to see if they are firm and plump. Cut a few open to see if the baby plant is pale and firm. Put some on a wet cloth in a warm place and count how many sprout over several days. If some sprout, the seeds were alive and only waiting.
items.why: A strong answer gives a way to check whether waiting seeds are alive, and says what the result would show. Putting them in good conditions is the fairest test.

items.p: A tamarind seed soaked in water for a day does not swell. A tamarind seed with a rubbed patch on the coat swells in the same time. What is the best explanation?
opts: The hard coat keeps water out until it is thinned
The seed has no baby plant inside
items.why: A thick hard coat is like a locked door. Rubbing thins the coat in one spot and lets water in. Picking 'no baby plant' is a mistake, because the untouched seed is alive and only locked.

items.p: A dormant seed is a dead seed that has not rotted yet.
items.why: False. A dormant seed is alive and is holding back until the right sign comes. A boiled seed is dead and will never sprout. A dormant seed will sprout once the right key comes.

items.p: Apple seeds taken straight from an apple sprout badly. After several weeks in a damp, cold fridge, many more of them sprout. What is the best explanation?
opts: The seeds need a spell of cold before they wake, which tells them that winter has passed
The seeds learn to love the cold
items.why: Many seeds of cold places stay dormant until they have been through a spell of cold. This stops them waking in autumn, when winter would kill the seedlings. Picking 'bigger' is not right. Cold changes the balance of chemical messengers inside the seed.

items.p: Match each part of a seed or seedling to its job.
pairs: keeps the baby plant safe and decides how fast water gets in
a message that tells a seed to wake
a message that tells a seed to stay asleep
helpers that cut starch into sugar
the green substance that catches sunlight
items.why: Each part has its own job. The two messengers pull in opposite directions, and a seed wakes when the balance tips towards waking.

items.p: A seed is 4 millimetres wide. A gardener's rule says to sow a seed two or three times as deep as the seed is wide. About how deep should this seed be sown?
items.why: Two times 4 millimetres is 8 millimetres. Three times 4 millimetres is 12 millimetres. So about 1 centimetre is right. Picking 4 centimetres means sowing the seed 10 times as deep as the seed is wide, which a small seed could not climb.

items.p: In the wild, an orchid seed is as fine as dust and has almost no food store. The seed can start to grow with no help at all.
items.why: False. An orchid seed has so little food that, in the wild, the seed grows only when a tiny fungus in the soil feeds the seed. The fungus is the seed's helper.

items.p: Tiny seeds are sown 8 centimetres deep in a tumbler of soil. None come up. When the soil is tipped out, there are long, thin, pale shoots that stopped under the soil. Explain what happened.
items.a: The seeds woke and grew, but the shoots had only a tiny store of food. Growing in the dark spends that food fast. They ran out of food before they reached the surface and the light, and could not make new food. They stopped growing and died under the soil.
items.why: A strong answer says that the seeds were alive and sprouted, and that the food store ran out before the light was reached.

items.p: Sort these seeds. Can they be dried and stored, or must they be sown fresh?
items: moong
Can be dried and stored
wheat
Can be dried and stored
chana
Can be dried and stored
mango stone
Must be sown fresh
jackfruit seed
Must be sown fresh
cocoa seed
Must be sown fresh
items.why: Dry-keeping seeds dry out on purpose and can wait for years. Wet-keeping seeds never dry out and die if they do, so they have to be sown soon after the fruit falls.

items.p: A moong seedling grown in a dark cupboard is 10 centimetres tall and pale. A moong seedling grown by a window is 5 centimetres tall and green. Which has more food left in the seed leaves?
opts: The window seedling, because the dark seedling spent more food on stretching
The dark seedling, because the seedling grew taller
Neither, because seed leaves hold no food
items.why: In the dark, a seedling spends their food on stretching to find light, and cannot make new food. The window seedling spent less on stretching and began making their own food. Picking 'the dark seedling' mixes up how tall a seedling is with how much food is left.

items.p: A family wants to keep chana seeds for sowing next year. Three neighbours give advice about storage.

views.says: Dry the seeds in hot sun for a week, then keep them in an open basket.
Dry them in the shade, then keep them in a closed jar in a cool cupboard.
Keep them in the fridge in a damp bag, so they stay fresh.

items.ask: Which plan would you choose? Give a reason from what you know about seeds. Then say one thing that another plan gets right.
items.a: A strong answer picks Rao Uncle's plan. Seeds live longest when they are dry and cool, so shade drying and a closed jar in a cool place is best. Selvi is right that seeds must be dry, but hot sun and an open basket can overheat the seeds and let in damp air. Mehra Aunty's cold is good, but damp is bad: a damp bag would wake or rot the seeds. A strong answer gives each plan its due.
items.why: Dry and cold slow the ageing of a seed. Heat and damp speed it up. A closed jar keeps out damp air.

items.p: A rough rule says each 5 degrees Celsius colder roughly doubles how long a seed stays alive. Suppose chana lasts about 4 years at 25 degrees Celsius. About how many years would chana last at 15 degrees Celsius? ____
items.why: From 25 down to 15 is 10 degrees, which is two steps of 5 degrees. Each step doubles the time. 4 doubled is 8, and 8 doubled is 16. It is only a rough rule, so the real answer will be different.

items.p: Which of these is not a key that wakes a sleeping seed? Rub on a rough surface, weeks of cold, smoke from a fire, boiling in water.
items.why: Rubbing thins a hard coat, cold tells an apple seed that winter has passed, and smoke tells some bush seeds that a fire has cleared the land. Boiling cooks the baby plant, so the seed never wakes.

items.p: Draw a moong seedling and a chana seedling, with the soil cut away so you can see under the ground. Show which one lifts the seed leaves into the air and which one leaves them under the soil. Label each.
items.a: Two cutaway pictures. In the first, a hooked stem has pulled two fat green seed leaves above the soil line. In the second, the seed leaves are still buried and only a shoot with small leaves is above the soil.
items.why: Moong lifts the seed leaves into the air. Chana and peas leave them under the soil.
items.art: An empty soil line drawn across the middle of a page, with a seed in the soil.

items.p: A mango stone, dried in a drawer for several months, can usually be sown later in the same way as a dry chana.
items.why: False. A mango seed is a wet-keeping seed, which dies on drying out and must be sown fresh. A dry chana is a dry-keeping seed and can wait for years.

items.p: Charles Darwin kept three spoonfuls of pond mud covered in his study, and counted 537 plants that grew from it over six months. What does this show?
opts: Mud holds many seeds that wait alive for a long time
Pond mud makes seeds grow faster
All the seeds were new that year
Plants can grow from mud without seeds
items.why: Mud with no plants in it still grew hundreds of plants. The seeds had been lying in the mud alive and waiting. Picking 'without seeds' is the old idea that plants appear from nothing, and the experiment shows that every plant came from a seed.

items.p: In a dry year, the seeds that woke first all died, and a few of the late seeds survived. In a wet year, the early seeds grew best. Explain why it helps a plant to have both early and late seeds.
items.a: Nobody knows in advance whether a year will be wet or dry. If a plant's seeds all woke early, a dry year could kill them all. If they all woke late, a wet year would waste the good weather. A mix of early and late seeds means that some seeds are well timed whatever the weather does. So the plant leaves young in every kind of year.
items.why: A strong answer says that the weather is unpredictable, and that a mix of wake-up times means that some seeds are right in any kind of year.

items.p: One test uses 10 seeds from a packet, and 7 sprout. Another test uses 100 seeds from the same packet, and 82 sprout. Which result is a steadier guide to the whole packet, and why?
opts: The test of 100 seeds, because a bigger sample is less changed by one odd seed
The test of 10 seeds, because 10 is easier to count
Neither, because a packet cannot be tested
items.why: With 10 seeds, one seed changes the answer by 10 percent. With 100 seeds, one seed changes it by 1 percent. A bigger sample is steadier. Picking 'easier to count' is true, but easy does not mean right.

items.p: Two rough rules say that each 1 percent less water roughly doubles how long a seed lives, and each 5 degrees Celsius colder roughly doubles it too. A batch of seeds is dried until it has 2 percent less water, and is stored 10 degrees colder. About how many times longer will the seeds live?
items.why: Drying by 2 percent doubles the life twice, which makes it 4 times as long. Cooling by 10 degrees doubles it twice, which is another 4 times. 4 times 4 is 16. The rules are rough, and they only work within limits, so the real result will differ.

items.p: Who should own a seed? Three people have different views.

views.who: A farmer who saves her seed every year
views.says: Seeds come from many farmers over thousands of years. Nobody should be able to stop me saving and swapping seed.

views.who: A company that spent years breeding a new variety
views.says: We did the work and paid for it. We should be able to sell our variety and protect it.

views.who: A scientist at a seed bank
views.says: Seeds are the base of our food. They should be kept safe for everyone, and anyone should be able to use them.

items.ask: Which view do you find most convincing? Give a reason from what you know about seeds. Then say what you think another person gets right.
items.a: There is no single right answer. A strong answer uses facts about seeds: farmers have saved and swapped seeds for thousands of years, and many people helped to shape every crop. It also says that breeding a new variety takes work, which people want to be paid for. A strong answer admits that the three views each protect something real.
items.why: Seeds were shaped by many people over a very long time, and new varieties also take real work. The question is a balance, and people still disagree about it.

items.p: A farmer has one bag of bajra seed and the first rain has just come. Plan how to sow the seed over the rainy season so that a dry spell cannot ruin the whole crop. Give a reason for each choice.
items.a: Sow about two-thirds of the seed after the first rain, and keep about one-third back. If a dry spell kills the first seedlings, sow the rest after the second rain. Digging a few places to check that seeds are alive helps to decide. Sowing in two lots spreads the risk.
items.why: A strong answer divides the seed into lots, gives a reason such as an unpredictable first rain, and says how the farmer would decide whether to sow the second lot.

items.p: A seedling that is shaded by a bigger plant stretches taller than a seedling in full sun. What is the best explanation?
opts: Light sensors in the seedling tell the seedling that they are in shade, so they stretch to reach the light
The seedling can see the sun
items.why: Plants have light sensors, and they respond to the amount and colour of light. A shaded seedling gets a different signal, and they grow taller to reach the light. Picking 'can see the sun' is a good guess, but a seedling has no eyes.

items.p: Which of these is the odd one out? Rice, wheat, maize, rajma.
items.why: Rice, wheat and maize are grasses. Their seedlings come up with a pointed sheath over the first leaf, and one thin seed leaf stays below. Rajma is a bean with two fat seed leaves, which lift into the air.

items.p: Why can seed banks not simply dry and freeze mango stones, as they do with chana?
opts: Mango seeds are wet-keeping seeds, which die when they dry out
Mango stones are too big for freezers
Mango seeds have no baby plant
Mango seeds only grow in cold places
items.why: A wet-keeping seed dies when the seed is dried. A dry-keeping seed can be dried and frozen and will wake up later. Scientists are trying new ways to keep wet-keeping seeds, such as freezing only the tiny baby plant.

items.p: Here are made-up counts of seeds with a root. At 12 hours: 3 seeds. At 24 hours: 12. At 36 hours: 20. At 48 hours: 22. Draw the line graph. Put the hours along the bottom and the seeds with a root up the side.
items.a: A line graph with points at (12, 3), (24, 12), (36, 20) and (48, 22). The line climbs steeply from 12 to 36 hours and flattens between 36 and 48 hours.
items.why: The graph shows a few early seeds, most seeds waking in the middle, and the line flattening as few seeds are left to wake.
items.art: An empty line graph with hours along the bottom and the number of seeds up the side.

items.p: A seed lab tests four lots of 100 seeds. The counts that sprouted are 82, 79, 85 and 82. The average number that sprouted in a lot is ____ out of 100.
items.why: 82 + 79 + 85 + 82 = 328. 328 divided by 4 is 82. So the average is 82 out of 100, or 82 percent.

items.p: Soaking a seed in water for a short time and then drying it again can make the seed wake faster the next time the seed gets wet.
items.why: True. This is called priming, and farmers and seed companies use it. It shows that the past of a seed can change how the seed behaves later.

items.p: A tiny seed stays dormant in the dark and wakes only when light reaches the seed. Explain how this helps the seed.
items.a: A tiny seed has only a little food. If the seed woke deep in the soil, the shoot would use up the food before reaching the surface. Light only reaches a seed that is near the top. So waiting for light means the seed wakes only where the shoot has a short climb and enough food.
items.why: A strong answer links the small food store to the depth and says that light is a sign that the seed is near the surface.

items.p: Match each result to what it shows.
pairs: Pond mud grows plants for six months
seeds can wait alive in the soil for a long time
Tamarind seeds swell only after a rub
a hard coat keeps water out
Bean sprouts are long and white
they are grown in the dark and stretch to search for light
8 of every 10 seeds sprouted in the seller's test
items.why: Each result points to an idea from the unit: waiting seeds, hard coats, the pale search in the dark, and the germination percentage.

items.p: A farmer sows seed after a light first rain. A week later, a hot dry spell kills every seedling. What should she do before she buys new seed?
opts: Dig up some seeds that did not come up and check if they are alive
Sow twice as much new seed on top
Pour water on the dead seedlings
items.why: Seeds that did not come up may still be alive and waiting for more rain. Digging a few up and checking costs nothing. Buying new seed first could waste money.

items.p: If you test 400 seeds, your result for the germination percentage will be exactly the same as the true percentage for the whole sack.
items.why: False. A bigger sample gives a steadier guess but not a perfect one. A test of 400 seeds is very good, though a different 400 seeds might give a slightly different number.

experiments.title: The Waking Curve: do all the seeds in a packet wake together?
experiments.context: This is the waking curve test. You put 30 moong seeds on a wet cloth and count how many have a root every 12 hours. Then you draw how the count grows.
experiments.question: Do 30 seeds on one wet cloth all wake at the same time? If not, how far apart are the first and the last?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess two things. How many hours will the first seed take to show a root? Will all 30 wake in the same hour, or one by one? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Plate A gets seeds from one packet. Plate B gets seeds from an older packet, or from the same packet if you have only one. Both plates get the same kind of moong, the same number of seeds, the same kind of cloth, the same water and the same warm place. So only the age of the seeds is different, or nothing is different if you have just one packet. You count at the same hours every time. A seed counts only when you can see a white root.
results_table: Hours since the seeds got wet
Plate A: seeds with a root so far
Plate B: seeds with a root so far
Plate A: new seeds with a root since last count

materials.item: 30 whole green moong seeds from the packet you use most (not dal)
30 more whole moong from the oldest packet you have. If you only have one packet, take 30 more from the same packet.
2 steel plates and 2 more plates to use as lids
2 pieces of clean cotton cloth or kitchen towel, each about the size of a plate
water in a cup, a pen, plain paper, a ruler and a marker
a clock or phone to tell the time

experiments.safety: Do not eat the seeds from this test. Wash your hands after touching damp seeds. Throw away any seeds that smell sour.

schedule.what: Guess. Wet the cloths and set out 30 seeds on each plate. Write the start time.
Count the seeds with a root after 12 hours and after 24 hours.
Count after 36 hours and after 48 hours.
Count after 72 hours.
Count after 96 hours. Draw the curve. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table at every count. Write the running total each time, which is all the seeds with a root so far. Then draw a line graph with hours along the bottom and seeds with a root up the side. Mark the hour when half of the seeds, 15, had a root.

setup.art: Two steel plates, each with a damp cloth and thirty moong seeds in three rows of ten, labelled A and B.
setup.caption: 1. Wet two cloths. Put 30 seeds on each, in three rows of ten.

setup.art: A second plate placed upside down on top of each plate as a lid, and a clock beside them showing the start time.
setup.caption: 2. Cover each plate. Write down the time the seeds got wet.

setup.art: A child counting moong seeds with small white tails on plate A, with a pencil and a table beside the plate.
setup.caption: 3. Every 12 hours, count the seeds that have a white root.

setup.art: A line graph shaped like a lazy S, with hours along the bottom and a mark showing when half the seeds had woken.
setup.caption: 4. Draw the graph. Find the time when half the seeds had a root.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: seeds with a root so far, out of 30 moong on a warm kitchen shelf
example_chart.x: Hours since the seeds got wet
example_chart.y: Seeds with a root so far (out of 30)
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up to show the usual shape. Your numbers will be different, and they will not match any other plate exactly.

flow.context: This is the first step of the waking curve test. You guess before you start.
flow.do: Show your child the seeds, the plates and the cloths. Ask for both guesses and the reasons. Write the guesses at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will count when thirty moong seeds wake up. How long will the first one take? Will all thirty wake at the same time? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Thirty seeds lie on one wet cloth. Will they all wake together? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think they will wake together, or one by one?
good: They are all from one packet, so they are the same.
Some seeds are bigger, so they may be slower.
Some may be older or have a damaged coat.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write both guesses in the table so you can look back at them on the last day.

flow.context: In this step you set up the two plates and start the clock.
flow.do: 1. Wet a cloth and squeeze it until no water drips. 2. Lay it flat on plate A. 3. Count 30 moong onto the cloth, in three rows of ten. 4. Do the same on plate B. 5. Cover each plate with another plate. 6. Write the start time.
flow.say: We start the clock when the seeds touch the wet cloth. Count thirty seeds in three rows of ten. Cover the plates so the cloth stays damp.
flow.kid: Wet two cloths. Put 30 seeds on each. Cover the plates. Write the time.
flow.parent: Keep both plates in the same warm place, away from direct sun. If you have only one packet, take plate B's seeds from the same packet. That is a useful test too, because it shows how different two plates from one packet can be. Do not eat these seeds. Start at about 8 in the morning or 8 in the evening, so that every count falls at an easy hour. Write the real time of each count and use those real hours on the graph. One child: do both plates. Two to four children: each child looks after one plate, one child reads the clock and one writes the numbers, and a second child checks every count. In hot weather over 35 degrees, look at the cloth twice a day, because wet seeds can turn sour.

check.q: Why do we start the clock when the seeds touch the wet cloth?
options: So every seed starts the count at the same moment
So we can count less often
check.why: A fair count needs one starting moment for every seed. Then the hours we write down mean the same for all of them.

flow.context: In this step you make the first two counts, at 12 hours and 24 hours.
flow.do: 1. Look at the clock. 2. Count the seeds with a white root on plate A. 3. Count plate B. 4. Write both numbers. 5. Cover the plates. Do this at 12 hours and again at 24 hours.
flow.say: Only count a seed when you can see a white tail. Write how many have a root so far, not only the new ones.
flow.kid: Count the seeds with a white tail. Write the number so far.
flow.parent: Leave the seeds where they are, so the rows stay clear. In a warm room, the first roots usually show between 12 and 24 hours, but these hours are only typical. A root counts when the white tail is at least as long as the seed is thick. In a cold room everything is later, so add counts at 60 and 72 hours. If the cloth feels dry, add a few drops of water.
flow.wait: Count again after 12 hours and after 24 hours

flow.context: In this step you make the next two counts, at 36 hours and 48 hours.
flow.do: Count both plates at 36 hours and at 48 hours. Write the numbers. Add a few drops of water if the cloth is dry.
flow.say: Is the number still growing fast? Or is it slowing down? How can you tell?
flow.kid: Count again at 36 hours and 48 hours. Is the number growing more slowly now?
flow.wait: Count at 36 hours and at 48 hours

flow.context: In this step you make the last two counts, at 72 hours and 96 hours.
flow.do: Count both plates at 72 hours and at 96 hours. Write the numbers. Note how many seeds still have no root.
flow.say: Some seeds are still asleep. Are they dead? How could you find out?
flow.kid: Count at 72 hours and 96 hours. How many have no root?

ask.q: How could you find out if a seed with no root is still alive?
good: Press a seed with a nail, because a live one is firm.
Leave the seed two more days.
Cut a seed open to see if the baby plant is pale and firm.

flow.parent: Seeds with no root after four days are usually either late or not viable. Leave them for two more days if your child is curious. A soft, grey or smelly seed is dead.
flow.wait: Count at 72 hours and at 96 hours

flow.context: In this step you turn your counts into a line graph, the waking curve.
flow.do: 1. Draw a line graph. Put hours along the bottom and seeds with a root up the side. 2. Mark a dot for each count on plate A. 3. Join the dots. 4. Mark the hour when 15 seeds had a root. 5. Do plate B in another colour.
flow.say: Look at the shape of the line. Where is it steepest? Where is it flat? What does a steep line mean?
flow.kid: Draw the graph. Join the dots. Mark where half the seeds had woken.
flow.parent: The line should be an S shape: slow, then fast, then slow. If your line looks more like a straight set of steps, that is fine. Write down what you actually found.

check.q: On a waking curve, the line climbs steeply in the middle and then goes flat at the end. What does the flat end mean?
options: Almost no new seeds are waking, because most have woken already
check.why: A flat line means the running total is not rising. Few seeds are left to wake. A flat end is normal, and a few seeds may still wake later.

flow.context: In this step you say what the test showed: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Then compare plate A with plate B.
flow.say: What do you think about seeds from one packet? What did you see in your counts? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Then compare plates A and B.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: seeds from one packet wake at different times. What I saw (made-up numbers): 4 seeds had a root at 12 hours, 15 at 24 hours and 29 by 96 hours, and the last one took four days. Why: each seed is a little different, so water and warmth reach each baby plant at different speeds. Seeds from the older packet are usually slower, and fewer of them sprout. If plates A and B were close but not equal, say that too. It shows how much two tests of the same seeds can differ.
flow.think: If all thirty seeds had woken in the same hour, what could go wrong in a field?

experiments.title: How Deep? A tiny seed and a big seed at three depths
experiments.context: This is a depth test. You sow tiny mustard seeds and big chana at 1, 3 and 6 centimetres deep and watch which shoots reach the top. Then you dig up the seeds that did not.
experiments.question: How deep can a tiny mustard seed and a big chana be sown and still reach the top?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many mustard seeds and how many chana will reach the top from 1, 3 and 6 centimetres down? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: All six tumblers have the same soil, the same amount of water and the same warm, bright place. Each tumbler has the same number of seeds, 8 mustard seeds or 6 chana. We compare mustard with mustard at different depths, and chana with chana at different depths. In each comparison only the depth changes.

materials.item: 6 clear tumblers or cups, each at least 12 centimetres tall (clear ones let you see roots at the side)
about 2 litres of loose soil from a flower pot or a packet of potting soil. Dampen it first in a bowl until it feels like a wrung-out cloth
24 mustard (rai) seeds
18 chana, soaked in water overnight
a ruler, a marker, masking tape and a spoon
a cup of water and a teaspoon
old newspaper for the dig
a bowl, and 6 small plates, katoris or pieces of polythene to cover the tumblers

experiments.safety: If a grown-up cuts bottles, cover the cut edges with tape. Do not eat the seeds that have been in soil. Wash your hands after touching soil. If anyone at home is allergic to mustard or chana, an adult should handle the seeds.

schedule.what: Guess. Soak the chana overnight and label the tumblers.
Sow the seeds at three depths.
Count the shoots up, 3 days after sowing.
Count the shoots up, 5 days after sowing.
Count the shoots up, 7 days after sowing. Tip out the tumblers and look at the seeds. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table at each count. Draw the tumbler that held the deepest mustard seeds, and show what you found when you dug them up. Draw a bar chart of the shoots up on the last count.

setup.art: Six tumblers in a row, labelled Mustard 1, Mustard 3, Mustard 6, Chana 1, Chana 3 and Chana 6, with chana soaking in a bowl beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Label six tumblers. Soak the chana overnight.

setup.art: A tumbler with 2 centimetres of soil, six chana pressed into the top of it, and a ruler measuring 6 centimetres of soil poured on top.
setup.caption: 2. Put in 2 centimetres of soil, the seeds, then soil to the right depth.

setup.art: A row of tumblers on a bright windowsill with green shoots coming up in some and none in others, and a child counting.
setup.caption: 3. Water a little. Count the shoots at the top 3, 5 and 7 days after sowing.
