setup.caption: 4. Tip out the tumblers. Look at the seeds that did not reach the top.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: shoots up after 7 days
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up to show a possible pattern. Your numbers will be different.

flow.context: This is the first step of the depth test. You guess before you start.
flow.do: Show your child the mustard seeds and the chana. Ask for guesses and reasons. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: Mustard seeds are tiny. Chana is big. We will bury both at three depths. Which will reach the top from deep down? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One seed is tiny and one is big. Which can climb up from deep down? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why might a big seed do better when sown deep?
good: Big seeds have more food.
Big seeds are stronger.
A big seed can push harder.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Children often say the big seed wins, but their reason is usually 'the big seed is stronger'. That is a good start. The food store is the real reason, and the test will show it.

flow.context: In this step you soak the chana and label the tumblers.
flow.do: 1. Soak 18 chana in water overnight. 2. Mark each tumbler with tape: Mustard 1, 3 and 6, and Chana 1, 3 and 6. 3. Collect about two litres of soil.
flow.say: The number on each tumbler is the depth in centimetres. We bury the seeds that deep. The chana needs to soak overnight.
flow.kid: Soak the chana. Label six tumblers with the seed and the depth.
flow.parent: Pick any soil that is loose and crumbly, such as the soil from a flower pot. Sandy soil or packet potting soil also works. If the tumblers have no holes, you must water very little, or the chana will rot.

flow.context: In this step you sow the seeds at three depths in six tumblers.
flow.do: 1. Wet the soil in a bowl until it feels like a wrung-out cloth. 2. Put 2 centimetres of damp soil in each tumbler. 3. Press 8 mustard seeds, or 6 chana, onto the soil, spaced apart. 4. Pour more damp soil on top, to 1, 3 or 6 centimetres as the label says. 5. Check each depth with a ruler. 6. Sprinkle 1 teaspoon of water on top. 7. Cover each tumbler and put all six in the same bright place.
flow.say: The depth is the soil on top of the seeds. Use a ruler to check. Water each tumbler the same amount.
flow.kid: Sow the seeds. Check each depth with the ruler. Give each tumbler the same water.
flow.parent: Do not press the soil down hard. Keep it loose. The tumblers need a bright spot that is warm, but out of hot direct sun. Water a little every second day, so the soil is damp but never soggy. The soil must be equally damp all the way down. If only the top is wet, the deep seeds get no water and the test is unfair. Take the covers off when the first shoots show. In hot weather the soil dries fast, so look every day. One child: do all six tumblers. Two to four children: each child takes one seed kind or one depth, one child measures with the ruler and one waters, all with the same spoon.

check.q: Why does every tumbler get the same soil, the same water and the same place?
options: So only the seed and the depth are different
So the soil does not get dirty
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes in each comparison. If one tumbler had more water, we would not know if depth or water caused the difference.

flow.context: In this step you count the first shoots, 3 days after sowing.
flow.do: Look at each tumbler. Count the green shoots that have come up through the soil. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Which tumblers have shoots? Which have none? Does this match your guess?
flow.kid: Count the green shoots in each tumbler. Write them down.
flow.parent: Mustard from 1 centimetre is usually up by now. Chana is slower. If nothing is up, that is normal for chana, so keep waiting.

flow.context: In this step you count the shoots again, 5 days after sowing.
flow.do: Count the green shoots again in every tumbler. Write the numbers in the table. Water a little if the soil is dry.
flow.say: Have any shoots come up from the deep tumblers? Which?
flow.kid: Count the shoots again. Add a little water if the soil is dry.

flow.context: In this step you count the shoots for the last time and dig up the seeds that did not reach the top.
flow.do: 1. Count the shoots for the last time. 2. Tip each tumbler out slowly onto newspaper. 3. Find the seeds that did not reach the top. 4. Look at each one. Is there a root? Is there a shoot? 5. Draw the longest pale shoot you find.
flow.say: Look at the seeds that never reached the top. Did they grow at all? What do you see?
flow.kid: Tip out the tumblers. Look at the seeds that did not reach the top.

ask.q: What do you notice about the shoots that did not reach the top?
good: They are pale and thin.
They grew a long way, then stopped.
The seed looks shrivelled, because the food was used.

flow.parent: Deep mustard seeds often did sprout, but the shoots are tiny. Tip each tumbler onto white paper and sift gently with a spoon. You may find thin, pale, curled shoots that stopped under the soil. The seed leaves are shrivelled because the food is gone. If the deep chana has not come up yet, wait two more days before you tip it out. Look for a pale curl 1 to 3 centimetres long, and use a magnifier if you have one. If you cannot find any, write that down. It is a result too.
flow.wait: Count 7 days after sowing, then dig

flow.context: In this step you say what the test showed: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: What do you think about seed size and depth? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a bigger seed can be sown deeper. What I saw (example numbers): 7 of 8 mustard seeds came up from 1 centimetre, none from 6 centimetres, and the chana came up from 6 centimetres. Why: a shoot grows in the dark using the seed's food. The chana has a big food store, and the mustard seed has a tiny one, so the mustard shoot ran out of food before the shoot reached the light. Your results may differ. Write down what you got.
flow.think: A tiny seed has little food. What does a tiny seed need that a chana does not need?

experiments.title: The Pale Search: what happens to a seedling that never sees light?
experiments.context: This is a light and dark test. You grow moong in a dark box and by a window, measure the shoots, and then move the dark ones to the window to watch what light changes.
experiments.question: How does a moong seedling grow in the dark, compared with one by a window? What happens when the dark one gets light?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After five days, which shoots will be taller, the dark ones or the window ones? What colour will each be? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both cups get the same kind of moong, the same number of seeds, the same tissue, the same water and the same warm room. Only the light is different. We measure the shoots the same way, from the seed up to the tip of the shoot.
results_table: Dark cup: shortest and tallest shoot (cm)
Window cup: shortest and tallest shoot (cm)

materials.item: 2 clear cups or tumblers, each about 12 centimetres tall
kitchen tissue paper to line the cups, two layers in each cup
10 whole moong seeds, soaked overnight
a cardboard box, a steel dabba with a lid, or a dark cupboard
a ruler, a marker and a cup of water

experiments.safety: Do not eat the seedlings from this test. Throw away any that smell sour. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Soak the moong the night before. Guess. Line two cups with tissue. Press 5 soaked moong between the tissue and the cup. Put one cup in the dark and one by a window.
Take a quick look and measure the shoots in both cups.
Measure both cups. Draw them. Then move the dark cup to the window.
Look at the moved cup. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table on days 3, 5 and 6. Draw one dark shoot and one window shoot side by side. Write the colour of each. On day 6, draw the moved cup.

setup.art: Two clear cups lined with kitchen tissue, each with five soaked moong seeds pressed between the tissue and the glass, and a little water at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Line two cups with tissue. Press five soaked moong in each. Add 1 centimetre of water.

setup.art: One cup inside a closed cardboard box in a cupboard, and the other cup on a bright windowsill.
setup.caption: 2. Put one cup in the dark. Put the other by a window.

setup.art: A child measuring a long pale shoot in a dim room with a ruler, and a short green shoot in the other cup.
setup.caption: 3. Take a quick look on days 3 and 5. Measure the shoots with a ruler.

setup.art: The pale cup placed on the windowsill next to the green cup, with small arrows showing the pale shoots starting to turn green.
setup.caption: 4. On day 5, move the dark cup to the window. Look again the next day.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: tallest moong shoot on day 5
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up to show a possible pattern. Your numbers will be different, and they depend on the warmth of your room.

flow.context: This is the first step of the pale search test. You guess before you start.
flow.do: Show your child the cups, the seeds and the dark box. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it in the table.
flow.say: We will grow moong in two places. One cup stays in the dark. One sits by a window. After five days, which will be taller? What colour will each be? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One cup stays in the dark and one sits by the window. Which shoots will grow taller? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think the dark seedlings will be shorter, or taller?
good: They have no light, so they cannot grow.
They are searching for light, so they stretch.
Plants like the sun, so the window ones grow best.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children guess that the window seedlings will be taller. Write the guess down. The result often surprises them.

flow.context: In this step you set up the two cups, one in the dark and one in the light.
flow.do: 1. Line each cup with a sheet of tissue. 2. Press five soaked moong between the tissue and the cup, halfway up. 3. Pour 1 centimetre of water into the bottom. 4. Put one cup in the dark box. 5. Put the other by a bright window, out of hot sun.
flow.say: The tissue holds the seeds against the glass. The water climbs up the tissue. One cup goes in the dark. The other goes by the window.
flow.kid: Line two cups with tissue. Press in five seeds. Add a little water. One goes in the dark.
flow.parent: Put the dark cup in a warm place that stays dark, such as a closed box in a cupboard. A box with the lid on is good. The window cup should be warm, but out of the hottest sun. Use two layers of tissue so that the water climbs well. A steel dabba left in the sun gets hot and cooks the seeds, so keep the dark cup in a cupboard. If the water turns cloudy or smells sour, pour it out and add fresh water. One child: look after both cups. Two to four children: each child sets up a pair of cups, dark and window, with 5 seeds each. Then compare the pairs. One child measures and one writes. Count only the seeds that grew. Measure from the seed to the tip of the shoot.

check.q: Why do both cups get the same seeds, the same tissue and the same water?
options: So only the light is different
So both cups look the same
check.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. If the dark cup had less water, we would not know if the dark or the water made the seedlings different.

flow.context: In this step you take a quick look and measure the shoots on day 3.
flow.do: 1. Check both cups after two days. 2. Add water to keep 1 centimetre at the bottom. 3. Open the dark box for less than one minute, in a dim room. 4. Measure the shortest and tallest shoot in each cup. 5. Close the box.
flow.say: Quickly now. Look in the dim room and close the lid again. What colour are the dark shoots?
flow.kid: Take a quick look at both cups. Measure the shortest and tallest shoots. Close the box.
flow.parent: A short look in dim light does no harm. A long look in bright light starts the greening, which is not what we want to test.

flow.context: In this step you measure on day 5, compare the two kinds of shoot and move the dark cup to the window.
flow.do: 1. On day 5, measure the shortest and tallest shoot in both cups. 2. Write the colour of each. 3. Pull out one dark shoot and one window shoot. 4. Lay them side by side on paper and draw them. 5. Move the dark cup to the window.
flow.say: Which shoots are taller? Which are paler? Which stand up straight? Draw them side by side.
flow.kid: Measure both cups. Pull out one shoot from each. Draw them side by side.

ask.q: What differences can you find between the dark shoots and the window shoots?
good: The dark ones are longer.
The dark ones are pale or yellow.
The dark ones are thin and floppy.
The window ones have open leaves.

flow.parent: Expect clear differences, though the numbers depend on the warmth. The dark shoots are usually longer, paler and thinner, with leaves still folded and a hooked top. The window shoots are shorter, greener and sturdier.

check.q: Why are shoots grown in the dark usually longer and paler?
options: They stretch to search for light and make almost no chlorophyll
They get more water in the dark
check.why: A seedling in the dark spends their food on stretching, to find light. With no light, they make almost no chlorophyll, which is the green substance, so they stay pale.

flow.context: In this step you see what one day of light does to the pale shoots.
flow.do: On day 6, look at the cup you moved. Look at the colour of the tips and the leaves. Compare with the window cup. Draw the moved cup.
flow.say: The dark cup has had one day in the light. What has changed? Look at the tips and the leaves.
flow.kid: Look at the cup you moved. What changed after one day in the light?
flow.parent: The tips usually show a tinge of green within a day, and the folded leaves begin to open. The long stems stay long. If you see no change, give it one more day.
flow.think: The pale shoots turned greener in a day. How did they know that the light had come?

flow.context: In this step you say what the test showed: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: What do you think about seedlings in the dark? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a seedling in the dark stretches to search for light. What I saw (example numbers): the dark shoots were 9 centimetres and pale, and the window shoots were 5 centimetres and green. Why: in the dark the seedling spends the food in the seed on growing long. Light tells the seedling to turn green and open their leaves.

experiments.title: The Locked Seed: what does a tamarind seed need before water can get in?
experiments.context: This is a hard coat test. You soak tamarind seeds with a hard coat, and you thin the coat of half of them first. Then you find out which ones drink.
experiments.question: Does a tamarind seed with a hard coat swell in water? Does thinning the coat make a difference?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After two days in water, which seeds will be bigger, the untouched ones or the rubbed ones? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both groups have 6 tamarind seeds from the same pulp, the same cup of water and the same warm place. The only difference is whether the coat has been rubbed. We press the seeds in both groups the same way, and weigh them if we have a scale.
results_table: Do the seeds feel soft or hard?
Press score of the 6 seeds at 24 and 48 hours (0 hard, 1 a little soft, 2 soft; most possible 12)

materials.item: 12 tamarind seeds, washed and dried, from a block of tamarind
a piece of coarse sandpaper or a metal nail file
2 small bowls or katoris, and water at room temperature
a small scale that weighs in grams (optional, see the shopping list)
a marker, paper and a pen

experiments.safety: A grown-up helps with the rubbing. Rub away from your fingers, over a plate, and do not blow the dust. Never use a knife, scissors or pliers to crack a seed. Tamarind seeds are small, so keep them away from toddlers.

schedule.what: Guess. Rub 6 seeds. Weigh both groups and put them in water.
Weigh both groups and press the seeds.
Weigh both groups. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Write the weights in the table at the start, after 24 hours and after 48 hours. Draw one seed from each group. Write whether each feels hard or soft.

setup.art: Twelve tamarind seeds on a plate, six marked with a dot on the bottom of the bowl and six waiting to be rubbed.
setup.caption: 1. Wash twelve tamarind seeds. Dry them on a cloth.

setup.art: A hand rubbing one tamarind seed on sandpaper until a dull patch shows on the shiny dark coat.
setup.caption: 2. Rub six seeds on sandpaper until the shiny coat turns dull. Do not rub deeper.

setup.art: Two small bowls of water, one with six rubbed seeds and one with six untouched seeds, beside a kitchen scale.
setup.caption: 3. Weigh each group. Put each in its own bowl of water.

setup.art: A child pressing a swollen seed with a fingernail, and the scale showing a heavier number.
setup.caption: 4. After a day and two days, weigh each group again and press a seed.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: weight of 6 tamarind seeds in grams
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up to show a possible pattern. Your numbers will be different. A scale that only shows whole grams will show small changes roughly.

flow.context: This is the first step of the locked seed test. You guess before you start.
flow.do: Show your child the tamarind seeds and the sandpaper. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it in the table.
flow.say: A tamarind seed has a hard, shiny coat. We will soak twelve seeds. Six get a rub first. Which will swell? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Six seeds get a rub. Six do not. Which will swell? Why?

ask.q: Why might a rub help a seed to swell?
good: It makes the coat thinner.
Water can get in.
It wakes the seed.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Some children think the untouched seeds will swell because they are 'whole'. Write that down.

flow.context: In this step an adult helps you rub a thin patch on six tamarind seeds.
flow.do: 1. Wash the seeds and dry them. 2. A grown-up holds a piece of coarse sandpaper flat. 3. Rub one seed on it until a dull patch about the size of a grain of rice shows. 4. Do this to six seeds. 5. Leave the other six untouched.
flow.say: Rub away from your fingers. Stop when the shiny dark coat turns dull and you see a lighter brown. Do not rub it all away.
flow.kid: Rub six seeds on sandpaper until the shine goes dull. Leave six alone.
flow.parent: The rub only needs to make one dull patch. Rubbing too deep will damage the baby plant inside. If the seeds still have sticky pulp on them, wash them well and dry them first, or the pulp will grow mould in the water.

flow.context: In this step you weigh both groups and start soaking them.
flow.do: 1. Weigh the six rubbed seeds and write the weight. 2. Weigh the six untouched seeds and write the weight. 3. Put each group in its own bowl. 4. Cover them with plenty of water. 5. Label the bowls.
flow.say: Weigh each group. Write the weight. Then cover them with water. Label the bowls so you know which is which.
flow.kid: Weigh each group. Cover each with water. Label the bowls.
flow.parent: Dry the seeds on a cloth before weighing. If your scale only shows whole grams, six seeds weigh about 3 grams. You can still see a doubling. If you have no scale, the press score is your measurement. Press each seed with a fingernail. Score each seed 0 (hard), 1 (a little soft) or 2 (soft). Six seeds can score 12 at most. Tamarind from a block may be too old to sprout. That does not matter, because this test is about water getting in, not sprouting. One child: do both groups. Two to four children: one team for the rubbed seeds and one for the untouched seeds, with one child to press, one to weigh and one to write.

check.q: Why do we weigh both groups at the start?
options: So we know how much each group changes
check.why: A weight at the start lets us work out how much extra water each group took in. Without a starting weight, we cannot tell if the seeds changed.

flow.context: In this step you weigh the groups again after one day and press the seeds.
flow.do: After 24 hours, take the seeds out and dab them dry. Weigh each group. Press each seed with a fingernail and give each seed a score. Put the seeds back in fresh water.
flow.say: Weigh each group again. Press the seeds from each bowl. Which are softer? Which group is heavier?
flow.kid: Weigh each group. Press the seeds. Which feel softer?

flow.context: In this step you take the last weighing, after two days.
flow.do: After 48 hours, weigh both groups again. Press and score each seed again. Write the weights and scores. Ask your child to say what they see.
flow.say: It has been two days. Which group has changed? How much heavier is it? Which is still hard?
flow.kid: Weigh both groups again. Which changed? Which is still hard?
flow.parent: Rubbed seeds usually swell within a day, and the weight typically goes up by half or more. Untouched seeds usually stay hard, though a few may swell slowly. If your results are different, write down what you saw, because that is a result too.

flow.context: In this step you say what the test showed: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: What do you think a hard coat does? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a hard coat keeps water out until it is thinned. What I saw (example numbers): the rubbed seeds weighed 6 grams after 48 hours and the untouched seeds stayed at 3. Why: water could get through the dull patch, but not through the hard coat. In nature, the coat is thinned by time, soil, fire, or by the gut of an animal that eats the fruit.
flow.think: In the wild, no one rubs the seed on sandpaper. What might thin the coat there?

activities.title: Iodine on a Seed: where is the food kept?
activities.context: In this activity, an adult helps you use iodine to find the starch in a seed. You find out which part of a chana holds the food, and what happens to the food when a seed sprouts.

materials.item: 12 chana (kala chana or kabuli chana)
a bottle of povidone iodine antiseptic solution (for example Betadine) or tincture of iodine from a first-aid box
a small cup of water, a spoon and a few cotton buds or toothpicks
a slice of raw potato and a slice of cucumber
a white plate and a kitchen knife (for the grown-up)
a cotton cloth to keep the sprouts damp

activities.safety: A grown-up handles the iodine and the knife. Iodine stains skin and clothes. Never taste it or the foods you test with it. Wash your hands afterwards. Do not use iodine if anyone is allergic to it. Keep the cup of iodine water away from small children.

schedule.what: Guess. Soak 6 chana overnight, then spread them on a damp cloth to sprout.
Rinse the sprouting chana every day until the test, and twice a day in hot weather. Keep the cloth damp.
Soak 6 fresh chana overnight.
Test the potato, the cucumber and both groups of chana with iodine. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

activities.record: Draw a chana opened in half and colour it as the iodine showed. Draw the soaked half and the sprouted half side by side. Write which part turned darkest. Score the darkness of the big halves and of the baby plant from 0 (no change) to 5 (blue-black), for the soaked chana and the sprout.

setup.art: A white plate with a slice of potato and a slice of cucumber, each with one drop of brown iodine solution, and the potato turning blue-black.
setup.caption: 1. Test the potato and the cucumber first. Starch turns iodine blue-black.

setup.art: Two chana split in half on a plate, one soaked overnight and one sprouted for six days with a long root.
setup.caption: 2. Split a soaked chana and a sprouted chana in half.

setup.art: A cotton bud dabbing diluted iodine on the cut face of the chana halves, with dark patches showing.
setup.caption: 3. Dab iodine on the cut faces. Look at which parts turn dark.

flow.context: This is the first step of Iodine on a Seed. You start some chana sprouting, and guess where the food is.
flow.do: 1. Soak six chana overnight. 2. The next day, drain them and spread them on a damp cloth. 3. Cover the cloth with a plate. 4. Ask your child to guess which part of a chana holds the food.
flow.say: Inside a chana there is food for the baby plant. Where do you think the food is kept? How could we find out? What do you think happens to it when the seed sprouts?
flow.kid: Soak six chana. Next day, put them on a damp cloth. Guess where the food is kept.

ask.q: Which part of a chana do you think holds the food?
good: The big halves.
The skin.
The baby plant in the middle.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. The chana on the cloth need six days to sprout. Rinse them with a little water and keep the cloth damp, but not soaked.

flow.context: In this step you look after the sprouting chana while they grow.
flow.do: Rinse the sprouting chana with a little water. Squeeze out the extra. Cover them again. Do this every day, and twice a day in hot weather.
flow.say: The chana are waking. Keep them damp. We will test them in a few days.
flow.kid: Rinse the sprouting chana. Keep the cloth damp.
flow.wait: Rinse every day until the test, and keep the cloth damp

flow.context: In this step you soak a second group of chana, for the test.
flow.do: Soak six more chana in water overnight. These are the soaked-only group.
flow.say: These chana will soak overnight. Tomorrow we will compare them with the sprouts.
flow.kid: Soak six new chana overnight.
flow.wait: Soak the night before the test

flow.context: In this step you test the iodine on two foods, to learn what starch looks like.
flow.do: 1. In a small cup, mix a few drops of iodine in water until it is the colour of weak tea. 2. A grown-up cuts a slice of potato and a slice of cucumber. 3. Dab a little iodine on each slice with a cotton bud. 4. Watch the colours.
flow.say: Potato is full of starch. Cucumber has hardly any. Watch the colours. This is our starch detector.
flow.kid: A grown-up mixes the iodine. Dab it on potato and cucumber. Which turns dark?
flow.parent: Use a little iodine, so the colour is like weak tea. Too much makes everything brown and hides the change. Povidone iodine such as Betadine is brown and gives a weaker blue-black than tincture of iodine. If the potato does not turn dark, add a few more drops. If it still does not, the iodine is too old.

check.q: Iodine turns blue-black on the potato and stays brown on the cucumber. What does that tell you?
options: The potato has starch and the cucumber has very little
check.why: Iodine turns blue-black when it meets starch. The potato is rich in starch, and the cucumber has hardly any. So now we have a starch detector.

flow.context: In this step you test a soaked chana and a sprouted chana with iodine and compare them.
flow.do: 1. A grown-up splits one soaked chana in half with a thumbnail or a knife. 2. Dab iodine on the cut face. 3. Look at the big halves and at the small baby plant. 4. Do the same with a sprouted chana. 5. Score the darkness of each part from 0 to 5. 6. Compare the scores.
flow.say: Look at the soaked chana first. Which part turned darkest? Then look at the sprout. Is it the same, lighter or darker?
flow.kid: Dab iodine on a split chana. Look at the big halves and the baby plant. Compare the sprout.

ask.q: What do you notice about the baby plant and the big halves?
good: The big halves went dark.
The baby plant stayed lighter.
The sprout is less dark than the soaked seed.

flow.parent: The big halves of the soaked chana usually turn deep blue-black, because they are packed with starch. The tiny baby plant is usually lighter. The six-day sprout may be a little paler, or dark in patches, because the seedling has used some starch. If both look the same, the seedling has used only a little so far. A plant takes a couple of weeks to empty a store. Write down what you really see. Test three chana from each group, because seeds differ. One child: score all six. Two to four children: each child scores and draws one chana while the grown-up dabs.

flow.context: In this step you say what the test showed: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: What do you think about where the food is kept? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the big halves hold the food, which is starch. What I saw: the big halves turned dark blue-black and the baby plant stayed pale. The sprout was paler than the soaked seed. Why: the baby plant uses up starch from the big halves as they grow.
flow.think: A sprout uses starch from the big halves. Where does the starch go?

activities.title: Packet Detective: read a seed packet and choose
activities.context: In this activity, you read three seed packet labels and decide which packet to buy. You work out how many seeds you need to sow to get the plants you want.

materials.item: paper and a pencil
a calculator, if you like
three real seed packets if you have them. If not, use the three made-up packets in the steps. You need to buy nothing.

schedule.what: Read the labels. Work out how many seeds to sow. Choose a packet and give your reasons.

activities.record: Write a table with three rows, A, B and C. For each, write the germination percentage, the age, how many seeds you would sow to get 30 plants, and what those seeds cost. Then write which one you would buy and why.

setup.art: Three seed packets on a table. Packet A says 90 percent germination, packed 10 months ago. Packet B says 70 percent, packed 2 months ago. Packet C is a loose bag with no label.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the three packets. Read each label.

setup.art: A child writing a table with three rows and columns for percent, age and seeds to sow.
setup.caption: 2. Write a table. Work out how many seeds to sow from each packet.

setup.art: A child choosing a packet and saying the reason aloud to a parent.
setup.caption: 3. Choose a packet. Give your reasons.

flow.context: This is the first step of Packet Detective. You read three made-up labels and guess which packet is best.
flow.do: Read the three labels aloud. Packet A: 90 percent germination, packed ten months ago, Rs 40 for 100 seeds. Packet B: 70 percent, packed two months ago, Rs 30 for 100 seeds. Packet C: loose seeds in a bag, no label. Ask which packet your child would buy and why.
flow.say: Three packets of moong seed. Packet A says ninety percent sprouted, packed ten months ago, and costs forty rupees for a hundred seeds. Packet B says seventy percent, packed two months ago, and costs thirty rupees. Packet C has no label. Which would you buy? Why?
flow.kid: Packet A: 90 percent sprout, packed 10 months ago. Packet B: 70 percent, packed 2 months ago. Packet C has no label. Which would you buy?

ask.q: Which packet would you buy, and why?
good: A, because it has the highest number.
B, because it is newer.
C is a risk, because we know nothing about it.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. There is no single right answer. Seeds lose their power to sprout as they get older, so a number measured ten months ago may be lower today. Ask what could be different now.

flow.context: In this step you work out how many seeds to sow, using the percentage on the label.
flow.do: 1. Write the three packets in a table. 2. Add columns called Seeds to sow and Cost. 3. You want 30 plants. Work out how many seeds to sow from A and from B. 4. Work out what those seeds cost.
flow.say: You want thirty plants. Packet A says ninety out of every hundred sprout. How many seeds should you sow to get thirty? Try Packet B too.
flow.kid: You want 30 plants. How many seeds from packet A? From packet B?
flow.parent: For packet A, 9 of every 10 seeds sprout. Sow 30 seeds and you get 27 plants. You need 3 more plants, which takes about 4 more seeds. So sow 34 seeds. For packet B, 7 of every 10 sprout. Sow 40 seeds and you get 28 plants. You need 2 more, which takes about 3 more seeds. So sow 43 seeds. At the prices above, 34 seeds of A cost about Rs 13.60 and 43 seeds of B cost about Rs 12.90. The costs are close, so age may decide the choice. Round up, because you cannot sow part of a seed. With two to four children, each works out one packet, then swaps to check.

check.q: A packet says 70 percent germination. You want 35 plants. How many seeds should you sow?
check.why: 70 percent means 7 of every 10 seeds sprout. For 35 plants, 35 is 5 lots of 7, so you need 5 lots of 10 seeds, which is 50 seeds. Sowing only 35 would give about 25 plants.

flow.context: In this step you think about what a label tells you and what it hides.
flow.do: Ask your child to think about what the labels do not say. Ask about age, how the packet was stored, and whether Packet C could be tested.
flow.say: A label tells you what happened in the seller's test. What does it not tell you? How could you test Packet C yourself?
flow.kid: What does a label not tell you? How could you test packet C?

ask.q: How could you test packet C yourself?
good: Put 20 seeds on a wet cloth and count.
Do it twice, to check.
Count after a few days.

flow.parent: The best answer for Packet C is to test it, as in the waking curve test: put 20 or 30 seeds on a wet cloth and count the roots after several days. A bigger test gives a steadier number.

flow.context: In this step you choose a packet and give your reasons.
flow.do: Ask your child to choose one packet. Ask for two reasons using numbers.
flow.say: Which packet will you buy? Give me two reasons. Use numbers.
flow.kid: Choose a packet. Give two reasons. Use numbers.
flow.parent: Any packet can be argued for. A good answer uses the numbers and also says what is unknown. For example: I choose B, because it is only two months old, so 70 percent is likely still true today. A has a higher number, but it was measured ten months ago.
flow.think: Would your choice change if packet A cost twice as much?

activities.title: Seeds That Cannot Wait: jackfruit or mango seeds, fresh and dried
activities.context: In this activity, you leave some jackfruit seeds to dry and sow others fresh. You find out if a wet-keeping seed can survive drying. Do this when jackfruit or mango is in season.

materials.item: 10 fresh seeds from a ripe jackfruit you have eaten, raw and never boiled or roasted, washed to remove the sticky pulp. If it is mango season, 6 mango stones with their husk on can do instead.
5 dry chana, for comparison
a small scale that weighs in grams (optional, see the shopping list)
2 pots or tubs with soil, and water
2 paper plates, labels and a pen

activities.safety: Jackfruit sap is sticky, so rub a little cooking oil on your hands first. Mango skin and sap can irritate some people's skin, so a grown-up handles the mango stones. Do not eat the seeds from this test, because they are tested raw. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Guess. Weigh 5 fresh seeds and 5 chana. Leave them to dry. Sow 5 fresh seeds.
Weigh the dried seeds. Sow the dried seeds.
Count the sprouts in both pots. If the Fresh pot is bare, wait two more weeks and count again. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

activities.record: Write the weight of each group at the start and after 7 days. Write how many seeds sprouted in each pot after three weeks.

setup.art: Five fresh jackfruit seeds and five chana on a kitchen scale, with the weights written on a paper.
setup.caption: 1. Weigh five fresh seeds and five chana. Write the weights.

setup.art: Two paper plates, one with jackfruit seeds drying in a shady airy spot and one in a pot of soil with seeds sown 2 centimetres deep.
setup.caption: 2. Leave five seeds to dry. Sow the other five fresh.

setup.art: Two pots labelled Fresh and Dried, with a few small shoots in the Fresh pot and none in the Dried pot.
setup.caption: 3. After a week, weigh the dried seeds and sow them. Compare the pots after three weeks.

flow.context: This is the first step of Seeds That Cannot Wait. You guess what drying does to each seed.
flow.do: Show your child the fresh jackfruit seeds and the dry chana. Ask what will happen to each when left on a plate for a week.
flow.say: Jackfruit seeds are wet inside, and chana is dry. We will leave some of each on a plate for a week. What will happen to the jackfruit seeds? Will they still sprout?
flow.kid: A jackfruit seed is wet inside. Chana is dry. What happens if you dry them? Why?

ask.q: What do you think drying will do to a jackfruit seed?
good: The seed will shrink.
The seed will still sprout later.
The seed will die.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children think that every seed can wait. Write down their reason. This activity only works in season, which is about April to July for jackfruit and April to June for mango. Out of season, skip it and watch the video instead. Do not buy dried or roasted seeds, because they will not sprout.

flow.context: In this step you weigh the seeds, leave some to dry, and sow the others straight away.
flow.do: 1. Wash the sticky pulp off ten fresh seeds. 2. Weigh five of them, and weigh five chana. Write both weights. 3. Put them on a plate in a shady, airy place. 4. Sow the other five fresh seeds 2 centimetres deep in a pot of damp soil. 5. Label the pot Fresh.
flow.say: Weigh five jackfruit seeds and five chana. Write the numbers. Sow five fresh seeds right away.
flow.kid: Weigh five jackfruit seeds and five chana. Leave them to dry. Sow five fresh seeds.
flow.parent: Keep the dried seeds out of the sun and away from rain. Keep the Fresh pot damp but not soggy, in a warm place. Pots need a hole in the bottom, or very little water. One child: look after both pots. Two to four children: one child owns the Fresh pot, one owns the Dried pot, and the others weigh, label and water.

check.q: Why do we sow five of the fresh seeds right away?
options: So we have a comparison with the dried seeds
check.why: Without the fresh seeds, we would not know if the dried seeds failed because they dried or because they were always unable to sprout. The fresh pot is our comparison.

flow.context: In this step you weigh the seeds again after a week of drying.
flow.do: After seven days, weigh the dried jackfruit seeds and the chana. Write both weights. Look at the dried seeds.
flow.say: A week has passed. Weigh them again. Which lost weight? What do the dried jackfruit seeds look like?
flow.kid: Weigh the seeds again. Which lost weight? What do they look like now?
flow.parent: The jackfruit seeds should be clearly lighter and wrinkled, because they were full of water. The chana should have lost almost nothing, because the chana was already dry. In a damp monsoon room the chana may even gain a gram. Write what you see.

flow.context: In this step you sow the dried seeds next to the fresh ones.
flow.do: Sow the dried jackfruit seeds 2 centimetres deep in the second pot of damp soil. Label it Dried. Keep both pots damp and in the same warm place.
flow.say: Now we sow the dried seeds. Same soil, same depth, same water. Only the drying is different.
flow.kid: Sow the dried seeds in the second pot. Label it Dried.

flow.context: In this step you compare the pots after three weeks.
flow.do: After three weeks, look at both pots. Count the shoots in each pot. Gently dig up a few seeds that did not sprout and look at them.
flow.say: Count the shoots in the Fresh pot and in the Dried pot. Which is better? What do the seeds that did not sprout look like?
flow.kid: Count the shoots in both pots. Dig up one seed that did not sprout.
flow.parent: Fresh seeds can take two to six weeks to sprout, so if the Fresh pot is still bare at three weeks, wait longer before you decide. Results can vary. Many seeds that dried for a week do not sprout. Write down what you actually find. With only 5 seeds in a pot, one seed changes the result a lot. If the Fresh pot is still bare at three weeks, count again at five weeks.

flow.context: In this step you say what the test showed: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: What do you think about seeds that dry out? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: jackfruit seeds cannot survive drying out. What I saw: the dried seeds lost a lot of weight and fewer sprouted than the fresh seeds. Why: a wet-keeping seed has no way to survive losing most of the water, so the seed must be sown fresh. If both pots sprouted equally, say that. Some jackfruit seeds survive some drying, and a longer drying time would show a difference.
flow.think: Chana can wait for years. A jackfruit seed cannot. What does each kind of plant gain from their way, and what does it cost them?

projects.title: My Seed Library: save, label and test your own seeds
projects.context: In this project, you save seeds from fruits your family eats, dry and label them, and test how many sprout. You make real seed packets with a germination percentage on each.

materials.item: ripe fruits with seeds from your kitchen: pumpkin, muskmelon, papaya, tomato or any ripe fruit you like
a tea strainer or sieve and a bowl of water
old newspaper or plain paper for drying
4 paper envelopes, or sheets of paper to fold into packets
a pen, tape, a cotton cloth and a plate
a ruler to draw a label

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the fruit. After touching papaya or chilli seeds, wash your hands and do not rub your eyes. Keep small seeds away from toddlers. Skip any fruit that someone at home is allergic to.

schedule.what: Choose four ripe fruits. Scoop out the seeds, rinse them and spread them to dry.
Turn the seeds over so they dry evenly.
Make and label the packets. Set up a germination test with 10 seeds of each kind.
Count the seeds that have sprouted.
Count again. Work out the percentage of each kind that has sprouted. Slow kinds such as papaya may need until day 21. Write the percentage on each packet.
Swap a packet with a friend or neighbour, and tell the story of your seed.

projects.record: A table for each seed kind: the fruit, the date saved, how many seeds sprouted out of 10, and the percentage. A neat label on each packet.

setup.art: Four ripe fruits cut open on a board, with seeds being scooped into a bowl.
setup.caption: 1. Choose four ripe fruits. Scoop out the seeds. Rinse them.

setup.art: Seeds spread in a thin layer on paper, in a shady, airy spot, with a child stirring them with a finger.
setup.caption: 2. Spread the seeds on paper in the shade. Turn them every day.

setup.art: Four small paper packets, each labelled with a name, a date and a germination percentage.
setup.caption: 3. Make a packet for each kind. Label each one.

setup.art: Ten seeds of each kind on a damp cloth on a plate, in four neat rows.
setup.caption: 4. Test ten seeds of each kind on a damp cloth. Count the sprouts.

flow.context: This is the first step of My Seed Library. You collect, rinse and spread out the seeds.
flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts the fruit open. 2. Scoop out the seeds into a bowl. 3. Rinse them in a strainer under slow running water. 4. Rub off the slimy coat. 5. Spread them on paper in the shade.
flow.say: Every fruit is full of seeds. Each seed is a baby plant. We will keep some of them. Rinse them well, so they do not go mouldy.
flow.kid: Scoop out the seeds. Rinse them. Spread them on paper to dry.

ask.q: Which fruit do you think has the most seeds?
good: Papaya.
Pumpkin.
Tomato.

flow.parent: Tomato and papaya seeds are covered in a slimy coat. Rinsing them under water and rubbing with a finger removes most of it. Choose ripe fruit. The seeds from unripe fruit, such as a young cucumber, often do not sprout well. Many shop vegetables are hybrids, so plants from their seeds may look different from the fruit you ate. That is a good thing to notice. Pumpkin and muskmelon are the surest to sprout. Tomato and papaya are slower and less sure, so pick at least one fast kind.

flow.context: In this step you dry the seeds so that they can be stored.
flow.do: Turn the seeds over with a finger once a day. Keep them in the shade where air can move. Wait until they feel hard and dry.
flow.say: Seeds dry best in shade, not in hot sun. Turn them each day. We want them dry, so that they keep.
flow.kid: Turn your seeds once a day. Keep them in the shade.
flow.parent: Dry seeds for about five days. A seed is dry when the seed feels hard and does not stick to the paper. Hot sun can overheat and damage seeds, so keep them in the shade.
flow.wait: Turn the seeds each day for about 5 days

flow.context: In this step you make a labelled packet for each kind of seed.
flow.do: 1. Fold four envelopes from paper. 2. Write on each: the name of the plant, the date, which fruit the seeds came from and the number of seeds. 3. Put the dry seeds in. Keep 10 seeds of each kind out for the test.
flow.say: A good seed packet tells a story. What is the plant? When did you save it? Where did the seed come from?
flow.kid: Make four packets. Write the name and the date on each. Keep ten seeds out for testing.
flow.parent: Add a line for the germination percentage, which you will fill in later. One child: make all four packets. Two to four children: each child takes one or two fruits and keeps their own packets, then you swap at the end.

check.q: Why do we write the date on a seed packet?
options: Seeds get older, and old seeds may not sprout as well
check.why: A seed's power to sprout drops with age, so the date helps anyone using the packet to know how fresh the seeds are.

flow.context: In this step you set up a germination test for each kind of seed.
flow.do: 1. Wet a cotton cloth and squeeze it. 2. Lay it flat on a plate. 3. Put 10 seeds of each kind in a row, with a paper label beside each row. 4. Cover with another plate. 5. Keep the cloth damp.
flow.say: We test ten seeds of each kind. A packet of seeds is only useful if the seeds wake.
flow.kid: Put ten seeds of each kind on a damp cloth. Label each row. Cover the plate.
flow.parent: Different seeds take different times. Pumpkin and melon often show roots in three to five days. Tomato takes five to ten days. Papaya can take two weeks or more. Keep the cloth damp, and be patient. If a seed grows white or grey fuzz, take that seed out, count that seed as not sprouted, and rinse the cloth.

flow.context: In this step you make the first count of your germination test.
flow.do: Count the seeds with a white root in each row. Write the numbers. Add a few drops of water if the cloth is dry.
flow.say: Which kind is fastest? Which kind is still asleep?
flow.kid: Count the seeds with a root in each row. Which kind is fastest?

flow.context: In this step you work out the germination percentage and write it on each packet.
flow.do: 1. Count again. 2. Write how many sprouted out of 10 for each kind. 3. Turn it into a percentage: 8 out of 10 is 80 percent. 4. Write the percentage and the date on each packet.
flow.say: Eight out of ten is eighty out of a hundred. That is eighty percent. Write it on the packet, like a real seed seller.
flow.kid: Count the sprouts. Turn each count into a percentage. Write it on the packet.
flow.parent: With only 10 seeds, one seed changes the answer by 10 percent. Tell your child that a real seed lab uses many more seeds. Slow kinds, such as papaya, may need more days.
flow.wait: Count again after about 4 more days

flow.context: In this step you share one of your packets with someone.
flow.do: Swap one packet with a friend or a neighbour. Tell the story of the seed: the fruit, the date and the test result.
flow.say: People have swapped seeds for thousands of years. Tell your friend the story of your packet.
flow.kid: Swap a packet with a friend. Tell the story of the seed: the fruit, the date and the test result.
flow.parent: Keep the other packets in a closed jar in a cool, dry place. Test them again in six months to see how a seed's power to sprout changes with time.
flow.think: Many families once kept their own seeds and swapped them. What would we lose if everyone bought seeds only from a few shops?

challenges.title: The Dry Vault: keep seeds dry in a damp season
challenges.problem: Your family keeps seeds for the next season, but the monsoon air in your kitchen is damp. Design a container that keeps 100 grams of chana dry inside a damp box for three days.
challenges.safety: Do not eat the chana or the salt packets after the test. A silica packet from a shoe box is not food, so keep it away from toddlers. Wash your hands afterwards. Keep the damp box away from small children.
constraints: Use only things from your kitchen, such as jars, bags, cloth, foil and rubber bands.
Each container gets 100 grams of chana and one salt packet. The salt packet is a level teaspoon of salt wrapped in a paper napkin.
Every container goes into the same damp box for three days.
You may not use a stove, sun or a heater.
Put one more salt packet alone in the damp box, with no container, and keep one in a dry cupboard. These two show wet and dry for comparison.
materials: a big plastic tub or steel dabba with a lid, to be the damp box
a small cup of water to put inside the damp box
400 grams of dry chana, in four portions of 100 grams
salt and paper napkins, for six salt packets (four for the containers, one for the damp box and one for the cupboard)
four containers to test, such as an open bowl, a jar with a lid, a plastic bag, a katori covered with cloth
a kitchen scale that weighs in grams (optional, see the shopping list)
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about keeping seeds dry. Seed banks keep seeds dry because water makes seeds age faster. You design the best container for a damp kitchen.
general: A jar with a tight lid, the way many families store dal and seeds.
A clean steel dabba with a rubber seal.
A jar with a spoon of dry rice or a silica packet inside to soak up any damp.
creative: Two containers, one inside the other, with a layer of dry rice between them.
A jar with a lid, wrapped in a plastic bag and tied, with a dry rice packet inside.
A pot of dry ash or clay under the seeds, as some farmers use, to soak up moisture.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own container. Draw it, build it and test it in the damp box. Which container kept the salt packet driest? Why do you think it did?

setup.art: Four containers on a table: an open bowl, a jar with a lid, a bag tied with a rubber band, and a katori covered with cloth, each with chana and a small salt packet.
setup.caption: 1. Put 100 grams of chana and a salt packet in each container.

setup.art: A closed tub with a small cup of water inside and the four containers sitting next to it.
setup.caption: 2. Put all four containers and a cup of water into the damp box. Close the lid.

setup.art: A child opening the tub after three days and holding up four salt packets, one of them clumped and damp.
setup.caption: 3. After three days, take out the salt packets. Which are damp?

flow.context: This is the first step of the Dry Vault challenge. You plan before you build.
flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the usual designs and the creative ones. Ask your child to sketch two or three containers of their own.
flow.say: A damp kitchen is hard on seeds. Water makes them age fast. How could you keep chana dry? Draw some ideas first.
flow.kid: Draw two or three ways to keep chana dry. Think about air and water.

ask.q: Why might a sealed jar keep the chana dry?
good: It keeps damp air out.
No air gets in.
The jar is waterproof.

flow.context: In this step you build your containers and put them in the damp box.
flow.do: 1. Weigh 100 grams of chana for each design, if you have a scale. 2. Wrap a level teaspoon of salt in a paper napkin and tie it. Make six packets. 3. Put the chana and a salt packet in each container. 4. Make the damp box with a cup of water inside. 5. Put one bare packet in the box, and keep one in a dry cupboard. 6. Put every container in the box. 7. Close the lid.
flow.say: Every design gets the same chana and the same salt packet. The salt packet tells us if damp air got in. Put them all in the damp box.
flow.kid: Build each container. Add chana and a salt packet. Put them in the damp box.
flow.parent: The damp box makes the air inside very humid. The salt is much more sensitive than the chana, so it shows the difference within a day or two. Do not eat the salt packets afterwards.

check.q: Why do we put a salt packet in each container?
options: Salt takes in water from damp air, so it shows if damp air got in
Salt makes the box smell nice
check.why: Salt soaks up water from the air and turns damp or clumpy. A dry salt packet means little damp air reached it. A wet one means the container let damp air in.

flow.context: In this step you open the damp box and see which design worked best.
flow.do: 1. After three days, open the box. 2. Take out the salt packets. Feel and look at each one. 3. Score each from 0 (dry and loose) to 3 (wet and lumpy). 4. If you have a scale, weigh each portion of chana. 5. Write which design kept the salt driest.
flow.say: Open the box. Which salt packet is dry? Which is damp or lumpy? Which container worked best?
flow.kid: Open the box. Feel each salt packet. Which is driest?
flow.parent: Salt pulls water from the air, so a damp packet shows that damp air got in. The bare packet should be the wettest and the cupboard packet the driest. A closed jar or steel dabba often keeps the salt driest, but many lids leak a little, so a few lumps are a real result. If everything looks the same, leave the box for one more day. Chana gains only a gram or two in three days. One child: test all four designs. Two to four children: each child builds one container, and one child sets up the damp box. Use the results to say why seed banks use airtight containers.
flow.think: A seed bank keeps seeds dry and cold. Which of the two is easier for a family to do at home?

challenges.title: The Rain Door: a seed that wakes only for a big rain
challenges.problem: In a desert, a small shower wets only the top of the soil, and a big rain soaks deep. Design a layer of sand over a seed so that a small shower does not reach the seed, but a big rain does.
challenges.safety: Use clean dry sand. Do not eat the seeds after the test. Wash your hands afterwards, and keep sand away from your eyes.
constraints: Use a clear cup about 7 centimetres wide and 12 centimetres tall.
Put a dry moong seed on a dry paper tissue at the bottom of the cup. The sand goes on top.
The small shower is 2 tablespoons of water, poured slowly. The big rain is about 1 cup (200 millilitres). If the cup overflows, use 150 millilitres.
You may change the depth of the sand, the kind of sand and the layers, but not the cup.
materials: 6 clear cups or cut bottles about 12 centimetres tall
dry sand or dry fine soil, about 1 litre. If the sand is damp, dry it in a tray in the sun for a day before you start. Clean sand costs under Rs 20 at a hardware shop.
paper tissues and 6 dry moong seeds
a tablespoon and a cup for measuring water
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about how desert seeds wake. A seed deep in dry sand stays asleep through small showers. Your job is to make a sand layer that works like that.
general: A deep layer of sand, about 6 centimetres, so a small shower soaks only the top.
A layer of coarse sand over a layer of fine soil.
A layer of dry soil that is packed down firmly, so water spreads sideways before it goes down.
creative: A layer of dry rice husks or dry leaves on top, which soak up a small shower and let a big rain through.
Three layers, each a different thickness, to catch different amounts of rain.
A paper tissue folded like a funnel in the sand, to guide a big flow of water down to the seed.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own layers. Draw your design, build it and test it with a small shower and then a big rain. Does your seed stay dry in the small shower? Does the seed get wet in the big rain? Why do you think so?

setup.art: A clear cup with a dry moong seed on a tissue at the bottom and a 6 centimetre layer of dry sand on top.
setup.caption: 1. Put a seed on a dry tissue at the bottom. Add a layer of sand.

setup.art: A child pouring two tablespoons of water slowly onto the sand, with a ruler showing how far the wet patch has gone.
setup.caption: 2. Pour on a small shower. Do not stir. Wait a minute.

setup.art: A child gently lifting off the sand with a spoon and checking whether the tissue at the bottom is dry or wet.
setup.caption: 3. Lift off the sand. Is the tissue dry or wet?

flow.context: This is the first step of the Rain Door challenge. You plan before you build.
flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the usual designs and the creative ones. Ask your child to sketch two or three designs, each with a different depth of sand.
flow.say: Rain in the desert is not always big. A seed deep in the sand stays asleep through a small shower. How can your sand do the same? Draw some ideas first.
flow.kid: Draw two or three ways to build the sand layers. Think about depth.

ask.q: Why might a deeper layer of sand keep the seed dry?
good: The water has further to go.
The sand soaks up the water on the way down.
The top layer holds the water.

flow.context: In this step you build a design and test it with a small shower.
flow.do: 1. Put a dry tissue at the bottom of each cup. 2. Put a dry moong seed on it. 3. Add sand to the depth of your design. 4. Pour 2 tablespoons of water slowly. 5. Wait one minute. 6. Lift off the sand a little at a time and check if the tissue is wet. 7. Measure how deep the dark, wet sand goes.
flow.say: Pour slowly, like a gentle shower. Wait a minute. Then lift the sand away. Is the tissue still dry?
flow.kid: Build your layers. Pour a small shower. Is the seed's tissue still dry?
flow.parent: Sand packs down and settles, so tap the cup gently to level it. The result depends on the sand, so expect to adjust the depth. If the small shower reaches the seed, try a deeper layer. Do not eat the seeds. Wet sand looks darker, so the ruler can measure how far the water went. One child: build and test all the designs. Two to four children: each child builds one design, and you compare the wet depths.

check.q: In the test, the tissue stays dry after the small shower. What does that tell you about the design?
options: The sand layer held the small shower in the top layer
check.why: A dry tissue means the water did not reach the seed. The sand soaked it up near the top. A seed in this design would stay asleep through a small shower.

flow.context: In this step you test your design with a big rain.
flow.do: 1. Make a fresh cup with the same design. 2. Pour 1 cup of water over the sand, in about 20 seconds. 3. Wait one minute. 4. Lift off the sand and check the tissue. 5. Measure the wet depth. 6. Write down what happened in each test.
flow.say: Now the big rain. Pour a full cup of water over the sand. Did it reach the seed this time?
flow.kid: Test the same design with a big rain. Does the seed get wet?
flow.parent: A good design keeps the tissue dry in the small shower and wet in the big rain. If the big rain floods the cup, that is also a result. Real desert rain soaks the ground deeply in this way. If you like, leave the big-rain cup for two days. The moong seed should show a root, and the seed from the small shower should stay dry and asleep.
flow.think: Among desert seeds that wake only in a big rain, many never wake at all. Is that a waste?

quiz.p: A tiny mustard seed and a big chana are each sown 6 centimetres deep. Which is more likely to reach the top, and why?
opts: The chana, because the chana has a bigger food store for the long climb
The mustard, because the mustard seed is smaller
Both, because all shoots reach the top
Neither, because the soil is too heavy
quiz.why: A shoot grows in the dark using the seed's own food. The chana has much more food than the mustard seed. Picking 'both' is a common guess, but a tiny seed buried deep runs out of food first.

quiz.p: Why are the bean sprouts in the market long and white?
opts: They are grown in the dark, so they stretch and stay pale
They are a different plant from moong
quiz.why: A seedling in the dark stretches fast and makes almost no chlorophyll. Growers use the dark on purpose. Picking 'dyed' is a guess, but the whiteness comes from the missing chlorophyll.

quiz.p: A seed lab tests 30 moong seeds. After four days, 27 of them have a root. What is the germination percentage?
quiz.why: 27 out of 30 is the same as 9 out of 10, which is 90 out of 100, or 90 percent. Picking 27 percent means using the raw count as the percentage.

quiz.p: Look at the graph of running totals. Between which two counts did the most new seeds wake?
quiz.why: From 12 to 24 hours the total rose from 4 to 15, which is 11 new seeds. From 24 to 36 hours it rose by 9. From 36 to 48 hours it rose by 3. The steepest part of the line is where the most seeds wake.
quiz.context: This graph is made-up. It shows how many seeds out of 30 had a root at each count of the waking curve test.

chart.title: Made-up example: seeds with a root so far, out of 30
chart.x: Hours since the seeds got wet
chart.y: Seeds with a root so far

opts: A living seed holds back from sprouting until the right sign comes
A seed has grown a first root
A seed has been stored in a jar
quiz.why: A dormant seed is alive but waiting. Picking 'died' is the usual mistake. A dormant seed will sprout when the seed gets the right key, and a dead seed never will.

quiz.p: Why does a seed packet show the date it was packed?
opts: Seeds get older and fewer of them sprout as the years pass
Seeds only sprout on the date written
The date tells you how deep to sow
quiz.why: A seed's power to sprout slowly drops with time. The date lets a buyer judge how fresh the seeds are. Picking 'only sprout on the date' misunderstands what the date means.

quiz.p: Which of these seedlings lifts the seed leaves up into the air?
quiz.why: In moong and rajma, a hooked stem pulls the fat seed leaves up into the light. In chana and peas, they stay in the soil. In rice, a sheath covers the first leaf, and one thin seed leaf stays below.

quiz.p: Two plates, each with 30 seeds from the same packet, give 26 sprouted on one plate and 28 on the other. What does this tell you?
opts: Even identical plates differ a little, because each seed is different
One of the plates was done wrongly
The packet has two kinds of seed
quiz.why: Small differences between plates are normal. Seeds are all a little different, so two samples will not match exactly. This is why labs test many seeds.

quiz.p: A jackfruit seed is dried in a drawer for a month, then sown, and does not sprout. A fresh jackfruit seed sown the same day does sprout. What is the best explanation?
opts: Jackfruit seeds are wet-keeping seeds that die when they dry out
Jackfruit seeds only sprout in winter
The drawer was too warm for the seed
Jackfruit seeds do not have a baby plant
quiz.why: A wet-keeping seed cannot survive drying out. A chana can, because chana is a dry-keeping seed. Picking 'no baby plant' is wrong, because the fresh seed sprouted.

quiz.p: Apple seeds sprout much better after weeks in a cold, damp fridge. What is the cold doing?
opts: The cold tells the seed that winter has passed, so waking is safe
quiz.why: Many seeds of cool places have a dormancy that only a spell of cold removes. This stops them waking before winter. Picking 'softens the coat' mixes up cold with a rub.

quiz.p: In a dry place, seeds in a field all woke at the first light rain. A long dry spell followed. What is the main danger of all seeds waking together?
opts: One dry spell can kill every seedling, and none are left
The seeds will be too crowded
The field will be too green
quiz.why: If every seed wakes at once, one bad stretch of weather can end them all. If seeds wake at different times, some are still asleep to try again. Picking 'too crowded' is a possible small problem, but it is not the main danger.

quiz.p: A pale seedling that grew in a dark cupboard is moved to a bright window. What changes first?
opts: The tips start to turn green and the leaves start to open
quiz.why: Light switches on the making of chlorophyll, and the seedling slows their stretching and opens the leaves. Picking 'the stem becomes longer' is the opposite. Light slows stretching.

applications: Seed companies test every batch and print the germination percentage on the packet, so a buyer knows how many seeds to sow.
Farmers sow extra seed to allow for the seeds that will not sprout, using the germination percentage to work out how much.
Farmers soak and dry seed before sowing, a trick called priming, so that the plants come up faster and more evenly.
Seed banks, such as India's national gene bank in New Delhi and the Svalbard vault, keep seeds dry and very cold so that they live for decades.
Nurseries rub or nick seeds with hard coats, such as tamarind, or soak them overnight, so that water can get in.
Forest restoration teams collect wild seeds and treat their dormancy, with cold, smoke or a rub, before sowing them to grow new forests.
Growers of bean sprouts and sprouted pulses keep seeds in the dark on purpose, so that the shoots grow long and pale.
Farmers in dry regions sow in two or three lots across the rainy season, so that one dry spell cannot ruin the whole crop.
Weed scientists study the soil seed bank to plan weeding, because weed seeds wake a few at a time for years.
Families and farmers dry grain well and keep it in airtight containers, so that the seed stays alive for the next sowing.
Plant breeders test many seeds from many plants, because a bigger sample gives a steadier answer.

open_questions.q: How does a seed add up water, warmth, light, cold and chemical signs, and decide when to wake?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found the sleep and wake messengers and many of the sensors. How the seed combines all the signs into one decision at the right moment is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: How can a seed sense the difference between a light shower and a big rain?
open_questions.why_open: Some desert seeds seem to know how much rain has fallen, and wake only after enough. Scientists have ideas about the chemicals in the coat, but nobody has a full explanation.

open_questions.q: How does a seed carry a memory of cold or of the mother plant's weather?
open_questions.why_open: Seeds from a plant that grew in a cool summer can behave differently from seeds of a plant that grew in a hot summer. Researchers are studying chemical marks on genes, and they do not yet agree on how much these marks explain.

open_questions.q: How much of the spread in wake-up times is a plan made over many generations, and how much is chance?
open_questions.why_open: Mathematics shows that spreading wake-up times helps in an unpredictable climate. It is very hard to tell, in a real plant, which part of the spread was selected and which part is only unavoidable small differences.

open_questions.q: Can we find a way to store seeds of mango, jackfruit and rainforest trees for decades?
open_questions.why_open: These seeds die if they dry out, so ordinary seed banks cannot keep them. Scientists are trying ways such as freezing only the tiny baby plant, but no method works for every kind yet.

open_questions.q: What happens inside a seed that is kept at about minus 20 degrees Celsius for a hundred years?
open_questions.why_open: Seed banks began only about a century ago, so nobody has waited long enough to know. The first tests of old stored seeds will take many decades.

maths.problem: On plate A, 24 of the 30 seeds had a root after 48 hours. What fraction of the seeds is that, in its simplest form? What is it as a percentage?
maths.explain: Divide both 24 and 30 by 6, which gives 4 out of 5. 4 out of 5 is the same as 8 out of 10, and 80 out of 100. So 80 percent of the seeds had a root.
maths.context: In the waking curve test, you count how many of 30 moong seeds have a root at each time.
maths.why_maths: A percentage lets you compare a plate of 30 seeds with a packet label or a test of 100 seeds.

maths.problem: The running totals of seeds with a root were 4 at 12 hours, 15 at 24 hours, 24 at 36 hours and 27 at 48 hours. How many new seeds woke in each 12-hour period? In which period did the most wake?
maths.answer: 4, then 11, then 9, then 3. The most woke between 12 and 24 hours.
maths.explain: The first period starts at 0, so 4 woke. 15 take away 4 is 11. 24 take away 15 is 9. 27 take away 24 is 3. The biggest number is 11, so the most seeds woke between 12 and 24 hours.
maths.context: In the waking curve test, each count is a running total, so the new seeds in each period come from subtracting.
maths.why_maths: A running total hides how many seeds woke in each period. Subtracting shows where the line is steepest.

maths.problem: A packet says that 80 percent of the seeds sprout. You want 60 plants. How many seeds should you sow?
maths.explain: 80 percent means 8 of every 10 seeds sprout. 60 divided by 8 is 7 and a half, so you need 7 and a half lots of 10 seeds. That is 75 seeds. A check: 80 percent of 75 is 8 tenths of 75, which is 60.
maths.context: Seed packets print a germination percentage so that a buyer can work out how many seeds to sow.
maths.why_maths: A ratio turns the germination percentage on a packet into a number of seeds to sow.

maths.problem: A rule of thumb says to sow a seed two or three times as deep as the seed is wide. A mustard seed is about 1 millimetre wide, and a chana is about 8 millimetres wide. What is the range of depths for each?
maths.answer: Mustard: 2 to 3 millimetres. Chana: 16 to 24 millimetres, which is about 2 centimetres.
maths.explain: For mustard, 2 times 1 is 2 and 3 times 1 is 3, so 2 to 3 millimetres. For chana, 2 times 8 is 16 and 3 times 8 is 24, so 16 to 24 millimetres. 10 millimetres make 1 centimetre, so that is about 2 centimetres.
maths.context: In the depth test, you sow mustard and chana at 1, 3 and 6 centimetres deep.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the rule with your own results shows if the rule fits the way real seeds behave.

maths.problem: A rough rule says each 5 degrees Celsius colder roughly doubles how long a seed stays alive. A batch of seeds lives 6 years at 25 degrees Celsius. About how long would the seeds live at 15 degrees Celsius, and at 5 degrees Celsius?
maths.answer: About 24 years at 15 degrees Celsius, and about 96 years at 5 degrees Celsius.
maths.explain: From 25 to 15 is 10 degrees, which is two steps of 5. 6 doubled is 12, and doubled again is 24. From 25 to 5 is 20 degrees, which is four steps. 6, 12, 24, 48, 96. So about 96 years. It is a rough rule, so these are rough numbers.
maths.context: Seed banks keep seeds cold because cold slows the ageing of a seed.
maths.why_maths: A doubling pattern shows why a few degrees of cold make a big difference to how long seeds live.

maths.problem: You put 30 seeds on a wet cloth at 7 o'clock on Monday evening. You make your last count 96 hours later. On which day, and at what time, is the last count?
maths.explain: 24 hours is one day. 96 divided by 24 is 4 days. Four days after Monday evening is Friday evening. The time of day stays the same, so it is 7 o'clock.
maths.context: In the waking curve test, you count at 12, 24, 36, 48, 72 and 96 hours after the seeds first touch the wet cloth.
maths.why_maths: Counting in hours and days helps you plan the checks and find the right times to look.

maths.problem: Six untouched tamarind seeds weigh 3 grams before soaking and 3 grams after two days. Six rubbed seeds weigh 3 grams before and 6 grams after. How much water did the rubbed seeds take in? How many times as heavy are they now?
maths.answer: 3 grams of water. They are 2 times as heavy.
maths.explain: 6 take away 3 is 3 grams of water. 3 grams doubled is 6 grams, so the seeds are 2 times as heavy. The untouched seeds took in no measurable water, which shows the hard coat keeping the water out.
maths.context: In the locked seed test, you weigh tamarind seeds before and after soaking them in water.
maths.why_maths: Weighing before and after turns the question 'did the seed drink?' into a number you can compare.

maths.problem: In the card game Wake or Wait, 13 of the 24 cards say SAFE. A woken seed on a SAFE card is worth 2 points, and on a DANGER card it is worth 0. A sleeping seed is worth 1 point. If you woke one seed on each of the 24 cards, about how many points would you win from those 24 seeds? What would 24 sleeping seeds be worth? Which is better?
maths.answer: 26 points from waking, 24 points from sleeping. Waking is a little better on average, but with much more risk.
maths.explain: 13 SAFE cards at 2 points is 26 points. The 11 DANGER cards give 0. 24 sleeping seeds at 1 point each is 24 points. 26 is a little more than 24, so on average waking is slightly better. But any single seed can lose, so players who wake everything at once can lose a lot on a bad day.
maths.context: In the game Wake or Wait, you choose how many seeds to wake before you know what the weather card says.
maths.why_maths: Counting how often the good card turns up shows why waking is a gamble and why spreading the seeds out protects the player.

roots.context: We counted how seeds wake, hour by hour, and found that seeds from one packet do not wake together. Now we ask what that spread in time tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Waking Curve test, thirty moong seeds from one packet lay on one wet cloth. They woke over several days, not in one hour. The first and the last were far apart. If all had woken together, one dry spell could end the lot. So the spread in time is part of how a group of seeds survives.
deep_truth.habit: We say a packet of seeds is 'the same', and we call the late ones slow, weak or dead. But the difference between seeds is not a fault. It is what keeps the group alive when the weather turns.
deep_truth.evidence: In the waking-curve test, seeds from one packet on one cloth sprouted over many hours, so the running total climbed slowly and not in one jump. In pond mud that Charles Darwin kept covered, 537 plants came up over six months. If your own plate looked different, write down what you saw.

three.who_am_i: Children of the same age do not all learn to walk in the same week. Some walk at nine months and some at eighteen months, and both are healthy. Differences in timing are normal in living beings.
three.what_is_life: A sleeping seed is alive. Living does not always look like growing. Sometimes living means waiting, and a late seed has not failed.
three.what_is_this_world: Nobody can predict the weather for a whole season. If every member of a group does the same thing at the same time, one piece of bad luck can end them all. A group whose members act at different times lives through it.

roots.thread: The thirty seeds came from one plant and share nearly the same instructions. Yet each seed wakes in their own time. So seeds from one source turn out different, and the group needs all of those differences. A field of bajra works like one living thing made of many seeds, some waking and some waiting. When one part fails, another part is ready.

teachings.teaching: A tree too big to hug grows from a tiny shoot. A journey of a thousand miles begins where you stand.
teachings.link: A whole field of bajra begins as a few seeds meeting water in the sand. The seeds that start late are still beginnings.

teachings.teaching: You see the earth dry and lifeless. Then when rain falls on it, it stirs, swells and puts out every kind of beautiful growth.
teachings.link: Dry sand holds seeds that stir and swell when enough rain reaches them. In the story The Second Rain, this is what the bajra seeds in the Thar desert do after the second rain.

teachings.source: A doha of Kabir, a poet of North India in the 1400s
teachings.teaching: Go slowly, my mind, for everything happens in its own time. The gardener may water with a hundred pots, but the fruit comes only when its season comes.
teachings.link: You cannot make a seed wake by pushing. Each seed has their own time, and watering more does not hurry the late ones.

science.text: In places where rain is unpredictable, plants that wake only part of their seeds each year leave more young over many years. Mathematics by Dan Cohen in 1966 showed why, and many desert plants behave this way.
How a seed adds up water, cold, light and chemical signs, and decides to wake, is still being worked out.

other_view.view: Part of the spread in wake-up times may be an accident. No two seeds can be built exactly alike, and not every difference has a purpose. Saying that seeds spread their risk puts a plan where there may only be chance, and it is hard to tell which is which.

how_we_found_out.story: Many people once thought that a seed which had not sprouted by the end of the season was dead, and that a field cleared of weeds was clean. Charles Darwin, an English naturalist, tested this in a simple way. He took three spoonfuls of mud from the edge of a pond and kept the mud covered in his study. He sowed nothing in it. Over six months, he pulled up each plant that grew from the mud and counted them. He counted 537 plants, of many kinds, from only three spoonfuls. The mud was full of seeds that had been lying there alive and waiting, some for a long time. He wrote this in his book On the Origin of Species, published in 1859.
